subject: Food and Bioprocess Engineering
selected_point: Determination of Yogurt Fermentation Effectiveness (pH Colorimetric Method)
posted_prompt: Take three test tubes, and add 2 mL of unfermented milk, fermenting milk, and fermented milk to each, respectively. Add two drops of bromothymol blue indicator to each tube.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Visual confirmation of yogurt fermentation stage via pH-dependent colorimetric response.
Minimum mechanism: Bromothymol blue must remain chemically intact and fully soluble in each tube; the three milk samples must represent successive points on one natural fermentation timeline (fresh milk → partially soured milk → finished yogurt), so pH falls steadily from roughly 6.6-6.8 (unfermented) through roughly 6.0-6.2 (fermenting, still inside bromothymol blue's ~6.0-7.6 color-change band) down to roughly 4.2-4.6 (fully fermented, well past the indicator's yellow threshold); indicator must fully dissolve and equilibrate to display a stable, non-diffusing color in each tube.
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0–2] Static wide shot showing three empty test tubes aligned left-center-right. [Frame 3–4] Pipette/dropper enters frame from top, dispenses two drops into left tube; drops contact liquid surface and disperse. [Frame 5–6] Dropper moves smoothly rightward, dispenses two drops into center tube: same contact/disperse behavior. [Frame 7–8] Dropper moves smoothly further right, dispenses two drops into right tube: same behavior. [Frame 9–10] Static hold: all three tubes fully in frame, colors stably displayed (green in the left tube, yellow-green/olive in the center tube, yellow in the right tube), no motion, no occlusion, full visibility of liquid column and color saturation. Perspective: fixed frontal close-up, eye-level, shallow depth of field focusing on liquid columns.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place three clean test tubes side-by-side.
2. Add 2 mL unfermented milk to left tube, 2 mL fermenting milk to center tube, 2 mL fermented milk to right tube.
3. Add two drops of bromothymol blue indicator to each tube.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
Left tube (unfermented milk) turns green; center tube (fermenting milk) turns yellow-green/olive; right tube (fermented milk) turns yellow.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Bromothymol blue is a pH indicator: yellow below pH 6.0, green near its neutral midpoint (roughly pH 6.8-7.0), and blue only above pH 7.6. Fresh milk is mildly acidic (~pH 6.6-6.8), so it reads green rather than blue. As lactic acid bacteria ferment lactose, pH falls steadily: partway through fermentation (~pH 6.0-6.2) the sample sits at the lower edge of the indicator's color-change band and reads yellow-green, while finished yogurt (~pH 4.2-4.6) is well below that band and reads a saturated yellow. The green → yellow-green → yellow progression tracks the drop in pH caused by lactic acid accumulation during fermentation.

pg_specification.level_1: No test tubes are visible, or fewer than three appear; no milk-like liquid is present in any tube; no dropper/pipette or bromothymol blue drops are shown; none of the three intended samples (unfermented milk, fermenting milk, fermented milk) can be told apart by tube position or labeling.
pg_specification.level_2: Only one or two test tubes appear, or a milk-like liquid is visible in fewer than three tubes; the dropper/pipette is missing, or indicator drops are never dispensed; the three tubes are stacked, overlapping, or otherwise not shown as three distinct, separately visible vessels, so the three intended samples cannot be told apart.
pg_specification.level_3: Three test tubes stand side by side, each holding about 2 mL of liquid at a similar fill height; the left tube holds the unfermented-milk sample, the center tube the fermenting-milk sample, and the right tube the fermented-milk sample, in the left-to-right order the storyline establishes; a dropper delivers exactly two visible drops into each tube in turn, six drops total, and each drop is seen landing on the liquid surface rather than the tube wall.
pg_specification.level_4: Everything required for a 3 also holds, and additionally: the dropper visits the tubes in the correct left-to-center-to-right order with no tube skipped, revisited, or given an extra/missing drop; the three tubes keep their original spacing and upright orientation before and after dosing; no extra tube, spilled milk, or duplicate dropper appears in the shot.
pg_specification.level_5: Everything required for a 4 also holds, and additionally: tube spacing, milk fill level, and dropper approach angle look visually identical across all three dispensing actions, as if the same dosing motion were simply repeated at each tube; nothing in the frame (glare, hand, cord) ever hides a tube during or after dosing; the scene contains no extra props beyond the three tubes, the milk, and the dropper/indicator.

scc_specification.level_1: The indicator produces no visible color change in any tube, or the same color appears in all three tubes; or the colors contradict bromothymol blue's real behavior (e.g., the right, most-fermented tube reads blue, or the left, unfermented tube reads yellow); there is no visible link between fermentation stage and hue.
scc_specification.level_2: Only one tube shows a color change while the other two stay colorless or unchanged; or the tube-to-tube color trend runs backward (the right, most-fermented tube looks less yellow / more blue-green than the left, least-fermented tube); or all three tubes converge on the same hue instead of three distinguishable ones.
scc_specification.level_3: After the indicator is added, the three tubes show three visually distinguishable hues that trend from green (or blue-green) on the left, through a yellow-green/olive middle tube, to yellow on the right, matching the order unfermented → fermenting → fermented; no tube shows a color outside this progression (e.g., no blue appears anywhere, since none of the milk samples is alkaline).
scc_specification.level_4: Everything required for a 3 also holds, and additionally: each tube's color is even from top to bottom (not visibly darker or a different shade near the bottom), with no cloudy, undissolved patch of indicator floating in any tube; the boundary between the three hues is a clean tube-to-tube difference rather than a gradual blend smeared across all three at once.
scc_specification.level_5: Everything required for a 4 also holds, and additionally: the left tube's green sits closer to blue-green than to yellow-green (consistent with the mildly acidic, near-neutral pH of fresh milk), the right tube's yellow looks fully saturated rather than pale (consistent with the much more acidic, fully fermented sample), and the center tube's hue sits visibly between the other two rather than matching either one; the three-tube hue order holds steady for the whole time all three are shown together, with no tube's color drifting into another's before the scene ends.

sc_specification.level_2: One tube's position shifts sideways between shots while the other two stay put; the dropper's path skips from one tube to another without passing over the tube in between; a drop leaves the dropper tip but never reaches the liquid surface, or vanishes just above it; the dropper's motion speeds up or stops in a way that doesn't match a smooth squeeze-and-release action; or the lighting or shadow on a tube shifts abruptly between frames (e.g., a shadow vanishing then reappearing), or a tube's cross-section visibly warps as if seen through inconsistent lens distortion.
sc_specification.level_3: The three tubes stay in the same positions and stand upright for the whole sequence; each liquid surface stays flat and still except for the brief ripple right after a drop lands; the dropper moves in one continuous path from the left tube to the center tube to the right tube; each drop can be seen falling and landing rather than appearing mid-air already merged with the liquid; no hard cut skips over the dispensing action.
sc_specification.level_4: Everything required for a 3 also holds, and additionally: the three tubes keep the same spacing and stand parallel to each other throughout, with no tube drifting closer to or farther from its neighbors; the dropper is held at roughly the same height and angle above each tube as it moves along the row; reflections and highlights on the glass shift only as much as the dropper's own movement would cause, with no unexplained new glare appearing on a tube the dropper hasn't reached yet.
sc_specification.level_5: Everything required for a 4 also holds, and additionally: the dropper's left-to-center-to-right movement reads as one smooth, evenly paced motion rather than speeding up, freezing, or resetting partway through; each drop's fall and the small ripple it makes on landing look physically ordinary (no oversized splash, no drop hanging motionless mid-fall); when the dropper passes in front of a tube it visibly blocks part of that tube rather than appearing to float in front of or behind the glass inconsistently from one moment to the next.

subject: Agricultural Engineering
selected_point: Immerse the roots of corn seedlings in red ink, wait several hours to allow transpiration-driven uptake, then cut across the stem and confirm that the xylem vessels appear red while the phloem remains colorless, resulting in a distinct visual effect.
posted_prompt: Immerse full-rooted maize seedlings in a container filled with red dye solution. After a period of time-lapse photography, remove one seedling and horizontally cut its stem with a blade. The structure of the cross-section is clearly visible, with particular emphasis on the internal vascular tissue structure.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Differential vascular transport capacity in maize stems, demonstrated by selective xylem dye uptake.
Minimum mechanism: Red dye must be water-soluble, non-toxic to living tissue, and molecularly excluded from phloem sieve plates; xylem vessels must be structurally open and lignified to permit passive capillary ascent; stem must be physiologically active (intact roots, hydrated) to sustain transpiration-driven flow.
(ii)Storyline: [Phase 1] Maize seedling fully immersed (roots submerged, shoot above liquid), establishing baseline state. [Phase 2] Static immersion for observable time (no motion except minor liquid meniscus adjustment), enabling dye uptake. [Phase 3] Seedling lifted vertically without shaking, preserving dye in xylem. [Phase 4] Blade contacts stem at consistent height and cuts horizontally in single fluid motion, revealing fresh anatomy. [Phase 5] Cross-section presented upright, centered, unoccluded, with lighting enabling direct visual discrimination of red xylem vs. colorless phloem/cortex/pith. Perspective remains fixed-side frontal view throughout; no camera movement, zoom, or re-framing between phases.
manual:
1. Experimental operation procedure: Submerge full-rooted maize seedling vertically in transparent container filled with red dye solution. Wait several hours (ideally overnight) to allow transpiration-driven capillary uptake of the dye through the xylem. Remove seedling. Horizontally cut stem near base with sharp blade. Place cut surface upright for viewing.
2. Observation of experimental phenomena: Cross-section shows discrete red-stained structures centrally located and radially scattered; surrounding tissues (cortex, pith, phloem) remain completely colorless—creating high-contrast visualization of xylem vessels only.
3. Summary of experimental principles: Xylem transports water and dissolved dyes upward via capillary action and transpiration pull; its lignified vessels retain red dye. Phloem transports sugars bidirectionally via living sieve tubes impermeable to large dye molecules—hence remains unstained.

pg_specification.level_1: No maize seedling, red dye solution, or container appears anywhere in the video; no blade or cutting action is shown; no stem cross-section is ever displayed.
pg_specification.level_2: A maize seedling, red liquid, transparent container, or blade appears, but not arranged as the procedure requires; for example the seedling is never submerged, the blade never touches the stem, no horizontal cut is shown, or no cross-section appears afterward.
pg_specification.level_3: A maize seedling with its root system submerged in red liquid inside a container (its shoot held above the liquid surface) is shown, a blade contacts the stem, a horizontal cut is performed, and a stem cross-section is displayed; but at least one element is wrong (the plant is clearly not maize, the liquid is not red, the cutting tool is not blade-like) or the sequence is broken (the seedling is lifted out and left in air well before the cut, or the cross-section shown belongs to a different, previously detached stem piece rather than the one just cut).
pg_specification.level_4: The maize seedling's root system (and the base of the stem) sits fully submerged in the red dye solution inside a transparent container, while its shoot and leaves remain above the liquid surface in open air, throughout the immersion phase; the seedling is then lifted out of the liquid; a blade visibly contacts the stem and executes one continuous horizontal cut; the freshly exposed cross-section appears in the same shot and viewpoint immediately afterward, without cutting to a different setup or substituting a different stem; no object is misidentified and no step is shown out of order.
pg_specification.level_5: The seedling's roots stay completely submerged throughout the full immersion period, with its shoot held continuously above the liquid surface, sustaining the transpiration pull that draws dye up through the xylem; it is then lifted straight up out of the liquid without shaking or splashing, and the blade begins the horizontal cut promptly after lifting, with no extended air-exposure delay; the cutting motion happens with the stem held steady, so the internal pattern is not blurred by camera or object motion; the resulting cross-section is centered and fully unobstructed in frame; and the whole sequence plays as one uninterrupted take, with no visible splice, zoom cut, or overlay breaking the path from container to exposed cross-section.

scc_specification.level_1: No color difference exists between xylem and phloem regions in the cross-section; the entire cut surface reads as uniformly red or uniformly colorless with no distinguishable vascular pattern; or, contrary to the real phenomenon, the outer tissue is red while the central vessels are colorless.
scc_specification.level_2: Red appears somewhere on the cut surface but is not confined to the internal vascular bundles; for example only the outer rind/epidermis is red, the red forms a diffuse wash across the whole section rather than sitting in distinct strand-like spots, or red shows up in clearly non-xylem tissue such as the cortex or the central pith.
scc_specification.level_3: Red appears as separate strand-like spots scattered through the stem's interior, roughly matching where maize vascular bundles sit, and the tissue immediately next to them stays colorless; but the effect is weak: the red is faint or low-contrast against the surrounding tissue, a few spots show reddish bleed into neighboring tissue, or a light pink tinge shows on the phloem side.
scc_specification.level_4: Red dye is confined entirely to the xylem strands: small, distinct, scattered points concentrated toward the stem's interior in the scattered-bundle pattern typical of maize; every other tissue region (phloem, cortex, pith, epidermis) is clearly colorless; the edge between each red point and the surrounding pale tissue is crisp enough to tell apart at a glance under normal lighting.
scc_specification.level_5: Beyond the sharp red/colorless split above, the red spots sit irregularly scattered across the section rather than forming one neat ring (matching maize's scattered-bundle anatomy rather than a ring-forming dicot stem); the tissue directly surrounding every red xylem strand, where the phloem sits, stays visibly colorless with no pink halo or bleed-through into it; and the red itself reads as a plausible aqueous dye tone (a red or pink food-dye/eosin look), not an unnatural neon, purple, or orange cast.

sc_specification.level_1: Severe continuity break: the seedling appears to jump directly from being in the container to already being cut, with no visible transition between the two; the cross-section appears before any cut is shown; the room lighting or shadow direction changes abruptly between the immersion shot and the cutting shot; the container or stem shape changes discontinuously; or the video is clearly a patchwork of unrelated shots.
sc_specification.level_2: Noticeable continuity break: the cut happens off-screen and the video cuts straight to an already-exposed cross-section; the seedling shifts position relative to the container or liquid level in a way the liquid itself doesn't match; the stem's orientation rotates or flips by more than roughly a quarter turn between the immersion shot and the cutting shot; a shadow suddenly points a different direction with no matching change in light source; or light passing through the container and liquid looks inconsistent with an actual liquid being present.
sc_specification.level_3: Minor continuity break: a hand or tool briefly blocks the view and the cross-section appears right after, but it's unclear whether that object is actually the blade; there is slight jitter or shake during the cutting motion; there is a brief flicker in brightness; or the cross-section is shown rotated by more than roughly 30 degrees relative to the stem's orientation just before the cut, though it is still clearly the same stem.
sc_specification.level_4: All level-3 conditions hold, AND the seedling stays fixed in position within the container throughout the immersion phase, then is lifted straight out along one continuous path with no abrupt jump before cutting begins; the blade approaches and touches the stem along one consistent path; the cutting motion is smooth and follows the stem's own axis; the cross-section appears immediately after the cut, viewed from essentially the same side and angle as the stem just before cutting; and there is no jump in lighting, shadow direction, or camera perspective between the immersion and cutting portions.
sc_specification.level_5: Beyond the above, there is no visible jump-cut or mismatched frame anywhere in the sequence; no motion blur obscures the red-versus-colorless boundary in the cross-section; the container's edges and the stem line up consistently with no odd parallax shift while the camera holds its view; the stem's proportions look natural throughout with no flattening or stretching; and the liquid's surface level in the container stays steady and undisturbed for as long as the seedling remains immersed.

subject: Electrical Engineering
selected_point: An RC circuit charges the capacitor, driving the LED brightness.
posted_prompt: On the workbench, there is a simple RC charging circuit: a battery, switch, and resistor are connected in series to charge a capacitor, and an LED is connected in parallel across the capacitor's two terminals; one hand toggles the switch to connect the battery.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Charging an RC circuit causes capacitor voltage to rise toward the battery voltage; because the LED is wired in parallel with the capacitor, its terminal voltage rises together with the capacitor, producing an observable increase in LED brightness as the capacitor charges.
Minimum mechanism: Battery, switch, and resistor must form a closed series charging path into the capacitor; capacitor must be shown charging from the battery through the resistor; LED must be connected across the capacitor's two terminals (a parallel branch alongside the capacitor, not simply chained end-to-end in the same single loop as the resistor); LED must be forward-biased so it can conduct once capacitor voltage exceeds its forward threshold; brightness must track capacitor voltage, increasing as the capacitor charges and leveling off as the capacitor approaches full charge.
(ii) Storyline: Frame 0–2s: Static wide shot: battery, switch, resistor, capacitor, and LED all laid out on the workbench with the LED visibly bridging the capacitor's two terminals; switch open; LED unlit. Frame 2–3s: Hand enters from bottom edge, approaches switch. Frame 3–4s: Hand contacts and toggles switch from open to closed (visible mechanical motion). Frame 4–9s: LED brightness increases from off through dim and medium toward bright, rising quickly at first and gradually slowing as it nears its peak, with no reversal; all components remain spatially fixed. Frame 9–10s: LED holds at its stable maximum brightness; hand fully withdrawn; no secondary events. Perspective: Fixed frontal or 30° angled view, full circuit always in frame, no occlusion of LED, capacitor, or switch during the transition.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place battery, switch, and resistor in series on the workbench, forming a charging path into the capacitor; connect the LED in parallel across the capacitor's two terminals.
2. Connect the components with wires so that closing the switch completes the battery-resistor-capacitor charging loop, with the LED bridging the capacitor.
3. With switch open, observe LED is off (capacitor uncharged, zero voltage across it).
4. Toggle switch to closed position with hand.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
LED begins unlit → gradually increases in brightness as the capacitor charges → stabilizes at a steady glow once the capacitor approaches full charge; brightness rise is smooth and non-instantaneous, slowing as it approaches its peak.
Summary of Experimental Principles
An RC circuit charges the capacitor: when the switch closes, capacitor voltage rises exponentially toward the battery voltage as current flows in through the resistor, with the resistor limiting the initial charging current. Because the LED is wired in parallel with the capacitor, the LED's terminal voltage rises together with the capacitor's voltage; once this voltage exceeds the LED's forward threshold, the LED conducts and its brightness increases smoothly as the capacitor continues to charge, leveling off as the capacitor approaches full charge and its voltage (and hence LED brightness) stabilizes.

pg_specification.level_1: Fewer than all five core parts (battery, switch, resistor, capacitor, LED) can be identified together in a single coherent circuit layout on the workbench, or the workbench itself is not shown.
pg_specification.level_2: All five parts can be identified but the wiring is wrong for this circuit: for example the LED is chained into the same single loop as the battery, switch, and resistor as though it were an ordinary series bulb, with no separate branch bridging the capacitor's own two terminals; or a component is swapped for something unrelated (e.g., a light bulb in place of the LED, a wire coil in place of the resistor).
pg_specification.level_3: Battery, switch, and resistor are connected in series into the capacitor, and the LED is connected across the capacitor's own two terminals (a visible branch alongside the capacitor rather than simply chained into the main loop); a hand enters frame and touches the switch, but the switch stays in the open position for the entire clip.
pg_specification.level_4: The battery-switch-resistor path into the capacitor and the LED's parallel connection across the capacitor are both correctly shown; a hand enters frame and visibly toggles the switch from open to closed (e.g., a lever moves or contacts meet), but the LED shows no brightness change at any point.
pg_specification.level_5: The battery-switch-resistor charging path and the LED's parallel connection across the capacitor are both correctly shown; the hand visibly toggles the switch from open to closed; the LED is dark before the toggle and visibly lit for at least one full second after it, with no extra components added, no component duplicated, and no LED shown with reversed leads/orientation relative to the capacitor terminals it bridges.

scc_specification.level_1: LED is already lit before the switch is closed, or never lights up at all after the switch closes, or jumps from fully dark to fully bright within essentially a single instant with no visible ramp, or blinks on and off repeatedly rather than tracing one continuous rise, or its color shifts away from a single steady hue partway through the charging interval.
scc_specification.level_2: LED switches on at full brightness immediately after the toggle with no perceptible ramp; or the capacitor is missing or is drawn as a different part (e.g., a second battery or a coil); or the resistor is missing or replaced by a bare wire; or the LED is shown wired only into the battery-switch-resistor loop with no visible bridge across the capacitor's terminals, so its brightness cannot plausibly be tracking capacitor voltage.
scc_specification.level_3: LED stays dark until the toggle, then visibly brightens over time instead of snapping on, and is shown bridging the capacitor's two terminals as required; but the brightening either reaches its full level almost immediately (within roughly half a second of the toggle) or never settles at a stable bright level anywhere within the ten-second clip, so the ramp duration doesn't read as a charging capacitor.
scc_specification.level_4: LED stays dark until the toggle, then brightens smoothly and continuously from off to a clearly bright, stable level with no flicker, dimming, or reversal partway through; the brightening rises monotonically across the interval with no stepwise jumps or plateaus; the final brightness holds for at least a short stretch before the clip ends.
scc_specification.level_5: In addition to the 4-point requirements, the climb visibly decelerates (rising quickly right after the toggle and progressively slowing as it nears its peak, matching the shape of a capacitor charging toward a fixed voltage), settles at a clearly bright peak, and holds that peak steadily for a sustained stretch of the remaining clip (roughly the last several seconds) with no later dimming, flicker, or color shift, and with no glow or swelling shown coming from the resistor or capacitor itself.

sc_specification.level_1: The LED or capacitor jumps to a new position between frames (e.g., appears mid-air then snaps onto the board), the switch resets to its open position after the hand lets go, the LED's brightness changes abruptly between one frame and the next with no visible transition, the workbench and its components change size or vanish partway through the clip, or the scene lighting or shadows shift abruptly between bright and dark with no lamp or camera movement to explain it.
sc_specification.level_2: The hand loses contact with the switch before finishing the toggle motion, the LED or capacitor shifts to a different spot on the board between the pre-toggle and post-toggle shots, the resistor or capacitor appears rotated by more than roughly 30 degrees without any hand touching it, a labeled part (e.g., a printed component label) blinks in and out of view, or a component's cast shadow vanishes and reappears pointing in a different direction between frames.
sc_specification.level_3: The hand keeps continuous contact with the switch through the whole toggle motion, and the battery, switch, resistor, capacitor, and LED all stay in the same relative positions and orientations throughout; however the hand's motion has at least one noticeable jump in speed (e.g., it suddenly speeds up or stalls), or the LED's brightening shows at least one visible backward flicker (a moment where it dims before continuing to brighten).
sc_specification.level_4: The hand's motion from approach through contact, toggle, and withdrawal reads as one continuous, evenly-paced motion; every component stays rigidly in place with no drift in position or angle; the LED's brightening rises without ever visibly dimming partway through; the camera view does not pan, tilt, or zoom, and no part of the circuit appears to shift relative to another as it would if the camera had moved.
sc_specification.level_5: All of the level-4 conditions hold, and in addition: the hand's approach, toggle, and withdrawal show no sudden speed changes anywhere in the motion; the LED's brightening traces a single unbroken curve from dark to peak with no visible pause, stutter, or reversal at any point; and the relative spacing between the battery, switch, resistor, capacitor, and LED looks identical in the first and last frames of the clip, with the camera framing unchanged throughout.

subject: Food and Bioprocess Engineering
selected_point: Determination of Protein in Food (Biuret Method)
posted_prompt: Take 2 mL of soymilk into a test tube, add 1 mL of reagent A of the biuret test, shake thoroughly to mix, then add 4 drops of reagent B, and shake again.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Visual verification of biuret test execution and positive result for protein in soymilk.
Minimum mechanism: Soymilk must contain sufficient intact peptide bonds; reagent A must be strongly alkaline (e.g., NaOH/KOH); reagent B must contain CuSO₄; mixing must enable complex formation; violet-purple chromophore must be stable and visually resolvable under ambient lighting.
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0–1] Static shot: empty test tube centered, soymilk container and two reagent bottles (A and B) adjacent in fixed positions. [Frame 2–3] Soymilk poured into tube: volume fills ~1/3, appearance light-beige and opaque. [Frame 4–5] Reagent A poured: clear stream, volume ~1 mL, followed immediately by vigorous swirling (meniscus distortion, liquid ascent/descent). [Frame 6–7] Four distinct blue drops descend into tube, spaced evenly, followed immediately by gentle flick-shake (small amplitude, rapid oscillation). [Frame 8–9] Violet-purple color emerges progressively from point of last drop impact, spreading uniformly to fill entire liquid column before video ends. All events occur from fixed frontal viewpoint; no camera movement; lighting constant; no occlusion of tube or reagent interfaces.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place 2 mL soymilk (light-beige, opaque liquid) into a clear glass test tube.
2. Add 1 mL reagent A (colorless, clear liquid) using a calibrated dispenser; shake tube vigorously to mix.
3. Add 4 drops reagent B (blue solution) from a dropper; shake tube gently to disperse.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
After step 3, the mixture develops a uniform violet-purple color throughout the liquid column.
Summary of Experimental Principles

subject: Civil & Environmental Engineering
selected_point: Adding salt to the slurry water leads to the formation of distinct agglomerates and sedimentation.
posted_prompt: Two transparent glass jars containing turbid muddy water are placed side by side; salt is added to the right jar. After both jars are briefly stirred, they are left undisturbed.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Coagulation-induced sedimentation in colloidal suspensions via electrolyte addition.
Minimum mechanism: Presence of fine suspended clay/silt particles stabilized by surface charge; introduction of Na+ ions neutralizes surface charge; loss of colloidal stability enables aggregation under Brownian motion and gravity; aggregates grow large enough to settle visibly within observation time.
(ii)Storyline: Frame 0–2: Two identical jars filled with homogeneous turbid water, side-by-side, static. Frame 2–4: Salt poured into right jar only; no salt contact with left jar. Frame 4–6: Simultaneous stirring of both jars; liquid rotates/swirls with visible vortex. Frame 6–10: Immediate cessation of motion; left jar retains uniform cloudiness; right jar shows progressive formation of suspended clumps (agglomerates) followed by downward migration and layered separation (sedimentation), all observed from fixed frontal viewpoint with full jar visibility.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place two identical transparent glass jars side-by-side on a flat surface.
2. Fill both jars with equal volumes of turbid muddy water (uniformly suspended fine sediment).
3. Add salt only to the right jar.
4. Briefly stir both jars identically with a clean rod.
5. Immediately stop stirring and leave both jars undisturbed.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
After stillness: right jar develops visible particle agglomerates and sedimentation (clear upper layer + dense bottom layer); left jar remains uniformly turbid with no clumping or layering.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Adding salt to slurry water compresses the electrical double layer around suspended clay particles, reducing electrostatic repulsion and enabling van der Waals attraction—leading to particle agglomeration and accelerated gravitational sedimentation.

Lamp brightness changes continuously: increases during one rotational direction, decreases during the opposite; warm-yellow incandescent glow intensifies and dims visibly; filament becomes brighter and more defined when bright, dimmer and less distinct when dim.

subject: Energy Engineering
selected_point: Direct Solar Radiation Heating Comparison between Asphalt Pavement and Lawn (Infrared View)
posted_prompt: Fixed infrared cameras captured two adjacent surfaces under noon sunlight: the left one was a dark asphalt pavement, and the right one was a green lawn, recording their temperature changes over time.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Differential solar heating due to surface albedo and thermal properties under direct insolation.
Minimum mechanism: Asphalt and lawn must be dry, exposed, unshaded, and at thermal equilibrium phase (i.e., sufficient time under sun to develop measurable divergence); infrared camera must render temperature as false-color with warm/cool polarity preserved.
(ii)Storyline: Frame opens on static wide shot of adjacent surfaces under bright overhead sun → asphalt and lawn fully visible, aligned horizontally, no occlusion → thermal contrast initiates within first 2 seconds (asphalt warms faster) → contrast intensifies steadily → peak divergence sustained through final 5 seconds → no interruption, no external interference, no lighting shift; viewer perspective is eye-level fixed camera, orthogonal to surface plane, capturing full thermal field without parallax.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Position fixed infrared camera facing south at solar noon.
2. Frame two adjacent ground surfaces side-by-side: left = dry asphalt pavement, right = healthy green lawn.
3. Record continuously for 10 seconds.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
Asphalt surface displays warmer infrared signature (e.g., orange/red false-color) while lawn displays cooler signature (e.g., blue/green false-color); difference is visible throughout and increases gradually.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Asphalt has low albedo and a relatively low specific heat capacity, so it absorbs most incident solar radiation and that absorbed energy produces a large, rapid rise in surface temperature; it also has no evaporative cooling to offset the heating. Lawn has higher albedo (reflecting more incoming sunlight), and evapotranspiration from grass blades and soil moisture removes energy as latent heat, keeping its surface cooler and slowing its temperature rise. Infrared imaging visualizes this differential surface temperature.

pg_specification.level_1: The dark asphalt pavement or the green lawn is missing from the shot, or only one surface appears; or the two surfaces are not shown side by side in the same frame (e.g., stacked one above the other, or shown in separate cuts); or the camera pans, zooms, or repositions instead of holding a fixed frame; or the scene shows nighttime, overcast sky, or an indoor setting instead of bright noon sunlight.
pg_specification.level_2: Either the asphalt pavement or the lawn is present and identifiable by its surface texture/shape (smooth paved surface vs. turf/grass blades) in the video's thermal rendering, while the other is missing, unidentifiable, or positioned so it is not adjacent to its counterpart (separated by a visible gap wider than either surface, or placed in a different shot). The camera holds a fixed viewpoint, but the side-by-side layout required by the prompt is not achieved.
pg_specification.level_3: Both the asphalt pavement and the lawn are visible side by side in one continuous shot, under bright overhead sunlight consistent with solar noon (short, near-vertical shadows and even ambient brightness), filmed with a fixed, unmoving frame; in the infrared camera's rendering, the asphalt is identifiable by its flat, paved texture/shape and the lawn by its grass texture/shape, with no swapped positions, missing surface, or incorrect count of surfaces.
pg_specification.level_4: Everything required at the 3-point level holds, and in addition: the asphalt-lawn boundary is unobstructed by any object or shadow that hides the adjacency; the two surfaces occupy roughly comparable width in frame (neither surface is more than about twice as wide as the other); and the fixed shot shows each surface's full extent without either edge being cropped out of frame.
pg_specification.level_5: Everything required at the 4-point level holds, and in addition: the asphalt's paved texture/shape is uniform, with no unexplained gaps, glare, or wet-looking sheen; the lawn's turf texture/shape is uniform, with no large bare-soil patches or an artificially uniform pattern that would suggest it is not real grass; the two surfaces share the same bottom edge/ground line with no vertical offset between them; and no unrelated object (person, vehicle, tool, or shadow-casting structure) intrudes into the frame at any point in the clip.

scc_specification.level_1: No temperature-difference effect is shown at all — the asphalt and the lawn display the same false-color hue/brightness in the infrared view, or the view is not color-coded for temperature at all; or the lawn appears warmer (redder/brighter) than the asphalt; or the scene shows a physically backwards state (e.g., the lawn steaming while the asphalt looks cold, or dew forming on the asphalt while the lawn looks hot).
scc_specification.level_2: Only one surface shows any thermal false-color signature while the other stays a flat, unchanging gray/neutral tone; or both surfaces show a color shift but with the asphalt cooler-colored than the lawn (reversed contrast); or the color change appears as an instantaneous switch rather than building up gradually as the clip proceeds.

subject: Geotechnical Engineering
selected_point: Strength Comparison Test of Lime-Modified Clay
posted_prompt: Drop two soil samples from the same height onto the ground, where sample A is pure clay and sample B is a mixture of lime and clay. Subsequently, observe and compare the damage experienced by sample A and sample B.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Lime stabilization enhances the mechanical integrity of clayey soils under dynamic loading.
Minimum mechanism: Pure clay has high water affinity and low tensile strength → brittle failure on impact; lime addition triggers pozzolanic reactions and cation exchange → reduced plasticity, increased inter-particle bonding → enhanced ductility and impact resistance.
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0–2] Static wide shot: two adjacent soil samples on platform, labeled or visually distinct (A brown, B pale gray), ground visible below. [Frame 3–5] Simultaneous release: both samples begin downward motion in parallel vertical paths. [Frame 6–8] Impact event: both contact ground in same frame; A visibly fragments/scatters; B remains whole and undistorted. [Frame 9–10] Static post-impact: side-by-side comparison clear, no motion, no recovery — damage difference fully exposed. Perspective: fixed frontal orthographic-like view; full samples and ground always fully visible; no occlusion.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place two identically sized soil samples side-by-side on an elevated platform: Sample A (pure clay, brown/dull), Sample B (lime-modified clay, pale gray/whitish). 
2. Release both samples simultaneously from same height onto a firm, level ground surface. 
3. Observe immediate post-impact condition.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
Sample A fractures, crumbles, or scatters into multiple pieces upon impact. Sample B remains intact, retains original shape, and shows no visible cracking or dispersion.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Lime modification reduces clay plasticity and increases cohesion and compressive strength, resulting in improved resistance to mechanical shock and impact-induced failure.

subject: Geotechnical Engineering
selected_point: Comparison of the Effects of Impact Compaction and Static Compaction
posted_prompt: Use two sandboxes filled with loose sand. A static pressure (weight of X) is applied to sandbox A, while a shock pressure of the same weight X is applied to sandbox B. Observe and compare the density and height of the sand in both sandboxes.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Granular soil densification under dynamic vs. static loading.
Minimum mechanism: Sand must behave as a cohesionless, frictional granular solid; impact must deliver transient kinetic energy sufficient to overcome inter-particle friction and induce rearrangement; static load must apply only sustained normal stress without acceleration-induced mobilization.
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0–1] Two labeled sandboxes with loose sand at equal initial height, fully visible in fixed side-by-side view. [Frame 2–3] Weight lifted above sandbox A and lowered steadily into contact, then held immobile. [Frame 4–5] Same weight lifted to identical height above sandbox B and released: contact occurs, brief surface deformation visible, weight rebounds/retracts. [Frame 6–9] Both sand surfaces settle; final state shows B uniformly lower and smoother than A. Perspective: frontal, eye-level, full-container framing; no obstructions; sand surface always in focus and evenly illuminated.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place two identical transparent sandboxes side-by-side, each filled with same volume of loose dry sand.
2. Gently place identical weight X onto center of sandbox A and hold still.
3. Drop identical weight X from short height onto center of sandbox B.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
- Sandbox A: sand compresses slightly, retains visible grain separation and slight surface mound.
- Sandbox B: sand compresses significantly, surface becomes flatter and denser, final height lower than A.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Impact compaction produces greater density increase than static compaction under equal force due to energy transfer inducing particle rearrangement and void reduction.

subject: Materials Science & Engineering
selected_point: Visual Comparison of Acoustic Properties of Construction Materials
posted_prompt: Using acoustic wave ripples (waveforms) to represent sound propagation, show sound waves traveling outward from a source toward a sponge block and a glass pane placed side by side, and continuing past each material to the far side.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Differential behavior of a propagating sound waveform when it passes a porous sponge versus a rigid glass pane, driven by how much each material damps (dissipates) acoustic energy.
Minimum mechanism: Sound must be shown as a propagating spatiotemporal waveform; the sponge's porous structure must convert acoustic energy into heat through internal friction, rapidly shrinking and stopping the waveform on its far side; the glass's rigid, non-porous structure must damp the wave far less, letting the waveform continue past it with only gradual amplitude loss over a much longer distance; both materials must be reached by the wave at the same moment from the same source.
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0-2] The acoustic source (e.g., a speaker cone) activates, visibly starting to vibrate; [Frame 3-5] a waveform ripple emerges from the source and travels outward toward the sponge block and the glass pane, placed side by side at equal distance from the source; [Frame 6-8] the waveform front reaches both materials at the same instant; [Frame 9-10] past the glass, the ripple continues on largely intact; past the sponge, the ripple visibly shrinks and stops within a short distance — all shown from a fixed frontal viewpoint with both materials fully visible and unoccluded throughout.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place a sponge block and a glass pane side by side, at equal distance from an active acoustic source (e.g., a speaker diaphragm).
2. Activate the source to emit a steady tone.
3. Visualize the sound as a real-time acoustic wave ripple emanating from the source and reaching both materials at the same moment.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
- Past the glass: the wave ripples continue on, evenly spaced and extending well beyond the pane, losing only a small amount of amplitude.
- Past the sponge: the wave ripples lose amplitude and their even spacing rapidly, and stop within a short distance of the sponge's surface.
Summary of Experimental Principles
The sponge's porous, fibrous structure dissipates acoustic energy into heat through internal friction as the sound wave moves through its open cells, causing rapid attenuation. The glass's rigid, non-porous structure has much lower internal damping, so sound passing it loses comparatively little energy, letting the waveform persist much farther on the far side.

subject: Materials Science & Engineering
selected_point: Visualization of Thermal Conductivity Comparison of Construction Materials
posted_prompt: Three large samples—rock wool (pale yellow), steel (silver gray), and wood (brown)—are displayed side by side, with dynamic red heat flow arrows indicating the rate of heat transfer. The focus of the image is on the contrasting movement speeds of the red arrows on the three samples.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Visual encoding of relative thermal conductivity via kinematic proxy (arrow speed). Minimum mechanism: Arrow speed must be a monotonic, perceptually resolvable proxy for material-specific k-value; viewer must infer conductivity ranking solely from comparative motion: no labels, numbers, or narration required.
(ii)Storyline: Frame 1: Static side-by-side display of three correctly colored material samples. Frame 2–10: Simultaneous onset of red arrows on all three, moving unidirectionally. Causal transition 1: Material identity → arrow speed assignment (steel→fastest, wood→intermediate, rock wool→slowest). Causal transition 2: Arrow speed difference → sustained visual contrast in displacement over time. Perspective constraint: Fixed frontal orthographic viewpoint, no camera motion, no occlusion, no depth layering: all samples and arrows fully visible and co-planar. Visibility constraint: Arrows must remain fully legible (color, shape, motion) against their respective material backgrounds throughout.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place three large rectangular samples — rock wool (pale yellow), steel (silver gray), and wood (brown) — side by side in a fixed frontal view.
2. Overlay dynamic red heat flow arrows on each sample, oriented identically (e.g., left-to-right), starting simultaneously.
3. Animate arrows to move continuously at speeds reflecting thermal conductivity: steel (fastest), wood (intermediate), rock wool (slowest).
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
Red arrows move continuously on all three samples; steel's arrow advances visibly farther than wood's arrow within the same visual duration; wood's arrow advances farther than rock wool's arrow, so wood is clearly slower than steel but faster than rock wool — creating unambiguous relative speed contrast across all three samples.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Thermal conductivity (k) determines rate of conductive heat transfer: steel (k ≈ 50 W/m·K) > wood (k ≈ 0.1–0.2 W/m·K) > rock wool (k ≈ 0.03–0.04 W/m·K); thus, higher-k materials permit faster apparent heat propagation, visualized as faster-moving arrows.

pg_specification.level_1: Fewer than three side-by-side material samples are shown; or none of rock wool (pale yellow), steel (silver gray), or wood (brown) appears in its correct color; or no red heat-flow arrows are present on any sample.

subject: Mechanical Engineering
selected_point: A mass-spring-damper system subjected to a brief impact by a mallet
posted_prompt: A mass-spring-damper system hangs vertically, suspended from a fixed frame above a workbench; a hand strikes the mass block with a rubber hammer briefly and then removes it, so that the mass is no longer subjected to external forces.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Underdamped free vibration of a single-degree-of-freedom mass-spring-damper system initiated by impulsive excitation.
Minimum mechanism: Mass must be elastically restrained (spring) and dissipatively coupled (damper) to a fixed support; impact must be transient (duration ≪ natural period); no sustained or secondary forcing after withdrawal.
(ii)Storyline: [Phase 1: Setup] Workbench visible; intact suspended assembly (mass + coiled spring + cylindrical damper) at rest. [Phase 2: Excitation] Hand enters frame holding rubber hammer; hammer contacts mass once with clear impact event (visible deformation/compression at interface); contact ends within ≤1/3 of total visible motion duration. [Phase 3: Isolation] Hand and hammer fully withdraw before mass displacement reverses; mass visibly detached and unsupported. [Phase 4: Response] Mass undergoes ≥3 vertical oscillations with monotonically decreasing peak amplitude; spring coils visibly expand/contract; damper rod moves in/out of housing in sync; no external interaction. [Phase 5: Settling] Motion ceases completely; mass returns to and remains at original equilibrium position. Perspective: Fixed frontal/slightly angled view showing full vertical travel of mass, full length of spring, and damper alignment; no occlusion of critical interfaces (mass-spring, spring-damper, damper-mount).
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Mount a mass-spring-damper system vertically from a rigid workbench.
2. Hold a rubber hammer in hand and strike the mass block once, briefly and perpendicularly.
3. Immediately withdraw the hand and hammer, leaving mass isolated.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
- Mass displaces at moment of impact.
- Mass then oscillates vertically with diminishing amplitude.
- Spring elongates/compresses synchronously with mass motion.
- Damper motion correlates with spring deformation, suppressing oscillation.
Summary of Experimental Principles
- A brief impact imparts initial kinetic energy.
- System responds via combined spring elasticity (restoring force) and damper dissipation (energy loss).
- Result is underdamped free vibration: decaying harmonic oscillation about equilibrium.

pg_specification.level_1: No mass-spring-damper assembly appears at all (no mass block, coil spring, or damper cylinder), and no hand or rubber hammer appears; or the apparatus shown is a different kind of system entirely (e.g., a pendulum on a string, or an object simply dropped and left to bounce on the floor).
pg_specification.level_2: The mass, spring, and damper are not shown connected as a single hanging assembly; for instance the hammer strikes an object not clearly attached to the spring/damper, the mass sits on a table rather than hanging, the hand/hammer never actually reaches the mass, or the workbench and the suspended assembly never appear together in the same shot.
pg_specification.level_3: The workbench, a vertically suspended assembly (mass block linked above to a coil spring and to a damper cylinder), a hand holding a rubber hammer, and a strike against the mass are all shown together; but the hammer lingers against the mass longer than a brief tap, or the hand doesn't fully pull away afterward, or the mass is never shown moving on its own once the hand leaves.
pg_specification.level_4: All score 3 elements hold, and additionally the hammer's contact with the mass reads as one short tap rather than a sustained push; the hand and hammer are clearly withdrawn from the mass before it starts swinging on its own; once withdrawn, nothing else touches the mass, spring, or damper for the rest of the shot.
pg_specification.level_5: All score 4 elements hold, and additionally the mass is struck exactly once, with no repeated taps; the hand's withdrawal is unambiguous: it moves clearly out of reach of the mass rather than lingering nearby; the spring and damper read as two recognizably separate, correctly connected parts (spring coils visible along the hanging axis, damper cylinder aligned with it) rather than an ambiguous blob standing in for both.

scc_specification.level_1: After the strike, the mass either doesn't move at all, or moves off in one direction and never swings back, or keeps swinging back and forth without ever losing height, or keeps swinging even while the hammer is still touching it.
scc_specification.level_2: The mass oscillates, but the physics is wrong in an obvious way: it starts swinging noticeably before the hammer makes contact, an oscillation that should be decaying instead repeats at the same size cycle after cycle, the spring and damper never visibly stretch/compress or move as the mass swings, or the mass appears to separate from the spring or damper mid-motion.
scc_specification.level_3: Once struck, the mass swings up and down at least twice, with each swing visibly smaller than the one before it; the direction of the first swing matches the direction the hammer pushed it; the mass stays connected to the spring and damper throughout; nothing touches the mass again once the hand withdraws, though the amount of visible decay may still be modest (for example, only two clearly shrinking swings, or the shrinking looking roughly even swing to swing).
scc_specification.level_4: All score 3 conditions hold, and additionally at least three swings are visible, each clearly smaller than the last; the spring's coils visibly stretch and compress in time with the mass's up-and-down motion; the damper's rod or piston shows its own motion moving in step with the spring; the mass comes to rest within a few more swings rather than continuing to oscillate indefinitely.
scc_specification.level_5: All score 4 conditions hold, and additionally the shrinking of each swing looks uneven in a physically sensible way: the drop in swing size between the first and second swing looks larger than the drop between later swings, rather than every swing shrinking by the same fixed amount; the spring and damper move together with the mass throughout, with no visible lag where one clearly moves before the others; by the end of the shot the mass has settled back at its original hanging position and stays there without further drift or swinging.

sc_specification.level_1: The mass, spring, or damper vanishes and reappears, or suddenly jumps to a different position; the spring or damper's length changes in one sudden jump rather than a continuous stretch or compression; the hand or hammer blinks in and out of the shot; the lighting flips abruptly between bright and dark with no visible cause; the workbench surface disappears or visibly warps; the mass passes straight through the spring or damper as if they weren't solid.
sc_specification.level_2: A major continuity break occurs: the mass keeps swinging while the hand is still gripping it; the spring stretches or compresses without the mass appearing to move accordingly; the damper's motion doesn't match what the spring is doing; the background or workbench shifts sideways or rotates partway through the shot; the shadows cast by the assembly point in a different direction partway through, as though the light source moved; part of the workbench edge disappears and later comes back.
sc_specification.level_3: The mass, spring, and damper keep a consistent size, shape, and position relative to each other throughout; the motion is continuous, without freezing, skipping, or stuttering; the shadows cast by the hanging assembly keep pointing the same way and stay about the same darkness from start to finish; the workbench stays fully visible and doesn't shift; nothing passes through anything else, though the mass's swinging path may show a little unevenness or the spring/damper axis may drift very slightly out of line.
sc_specification.level_4: All score 3 conditions hold, and additionally the spring's centerline stays lined up with the direction the mass moves throughout the swing; the damper's outer housing stays fixed relative to the workbench while only its internal rod moves; the hand's withdrawal is smooth, without sudden jerks or speed changes; the framing doesn't drift or re-center, so the bench and assembly stay in the same place in the shot.
sc_specification.level_5: All score 4 conditions hold, and additionally the mass, spring coils, and damper housing never stretch or squash out of their normal proportions during the motion; the sequence never repeats or skips a moment of the swing in a way that breaks the flow of motion; no part of the mass, spring, or damper is ever hidden behind the hand or hammer after they've withdrawn; the workbench edges and any background objects stay exactly where they started, confirming the camera never moved.

subject: Communications Engineering
selected_point: AM radio transmission: The microphone modulates the carrier amplitude, as observed on the oscilloscope.
posted_prompt: On the test bench, a microphone is connected to an AM transmitter and antenna; when a person speaks softly and then loudly into the microphone, the oscilloscope displays the corresponding signals.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Amplitude modulation via acoustic pressure driving microphone diaphragm, which linearly varies transmitter gain to produce time-varying envelope on carrier wave.
Minimum mechanism: Microphone must be functional (diaphragm responsive), transmitter must be AM-mode (not FM or unmodulated), oscilloscope must be AC-coupled and triggered to display envelope, and audio input must drive sufficient voltage swing to visibly alter carrier amplitude.
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0–2] Person silent, microphone idle, oscilloscope shows steady carrier waveform (constant amplitude). [Frame 2–5] Person begins soft speech → oscilloscope envelope begins smooth, proportional contraction. [Frame 5–8] Person transitions to loud speech → envelope expands smoothly and fully, maintaining carrier frequency integrity. [Frame 8–10] Person ends loud speech → envelope contracts smoothly back toward baseline. All events occur from fixed frontal viewpoint; microphone, transmitter, antenna, and oscilloscope remain fully visible and spatially anchored; no cutaways, zooms, or perspective shifts.

Experimental Procedure
1. Connect microphone to AM transmitter input; connect transmitter output to antenna and oscilloscope input.
2. Person speaks softly, then loudly into microphone.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
Oscilloscope displays a continuous carrier waveform whose amplitude increases visibly during loud speech and decreases visibly during soft speech.
Summary of Experimental Principles
AM radio transmission: The microphone modulates the carrier amplitude, as observed on the oscilloscope.

subject: Aerospace Engineering
selected_point: Smoke lines around an airfoil in a wind tunnel
posted_prompt: In the wind tunnel, a thin airfoil is horizontally installed, and smoke lines are continuously injected upstream under steady airflow conditions, while the airfoil is gradually rotated to increase the angle of attack.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Steady-state visualization of streamlines via smoke wires in a wind tunnel, demonstrating how angle-of-attack variation alters streamline geometry around a lifting body.
Minimum mechanism: Continuous smoke injection + steady laminar airflow + rigid-body airfoil rotation about fixed axis + optical transparency of tunnel walls + absence of unsteady disturbances (e.g., gusts, vibrations, vortex shedding).
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0–2] Airfoil horizontal; smoke lines straight, parallel, uniformly spaced upstream; no distortion near airfoil. [Frame 3–5] Rotation begins; smoke lines near leading edge start converging and curving smoothly around both surfaces; stagnation point appears. [Frame 6–8] Rotation continues; upper-surface lines arch more sharply; lower-surface lines compress; stagnation point migrates downward; asymmetry intensifies. [Frame 9–10] Final orientation reached; all smoke lines remain attached, continuous, and geometrically consistent with airfoil contour: no separation, no detachment, no turbulence. Perspective: Fixed frontal/slightly oblique view showing full airfoil, upstream injection zone, and adjacent tunnel walls; no occlusion; lighting uniform and front-dominant to ensure visibility of smoke contrast.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Mount thin, symmetrical airfoil horizontally inside transparent-walled wind tunnel test section.
2. Initiate steady, laminar airflow; confirm uniform background flow.
3. Begin continuous smoke injection upstream of airfoil.
4. While smoke flows steadily, gradually rotate airfoil about its quarter-chord axis to increase angle of attack.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
- Smoke lines remain straight and parallel upstream of airfoil.
- Near airfoil, smoke lines bend smoothly around upper and lower surfaces.
- As angle of attack increases, bending becomes increasingly asymmetric: stronger curvature above, compression below.
- A visible stagnation point forms near leading edge and shifts downward with rotation.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Smoke lines visualize instantaneous streamlines in steady, incompressible flow. Their curvature reveals local pressure gradients; asymmetric bending indicates lift generation. Increasing angle of attack amplifies circulation and adverse pressure gradient on upper surface, altering streamline topology per inviscid and boundary-layer theory.

pg_specification.level_1: No airfoil present; no smoke injection visible; no rotation motion observed; no steady airflow indication (e.g., uniform background flow cues); scene does not depict a wind tunnel environment.
pg_specification.level_2: Airfoil is present and horizontally oriented at start, but smoke lines are absent or static/non-flowing; rotation action is missing or replaced by translation/translation-only motion; wind tunnel enclosure (transparent walls, test section boundaries) is partially or fully missing.
pg_specification.level_3: Airfoil is present, initially horizontal; smoke lines are continuously injected upstream and visibly stream downstream; airflow appears steady (no turbulence bursts, pulsation, or chaotic eddies in undisturbed region); airfoil begins rotation (orientation visibly changes from horizontal toward higher angle), and this rotation occurs *while* smoke lines remain active and flowing.
pg_specification.level_4: All elements of 3-score are present, AND the airfoil remains fixed in position (no lateral/vertical translation during rotation); smoke injection point is upstream of airfoil (not at leading edge or on surface); smoke lines maintain continuity and coherence upstream of airfoil throughout rotation; viewpoint is fixed, showing full airfoil and adjacent flow field without cropping or occlusion.

scc_specification.level_1: Smoke lines do not respond to airfoil orientation; smoke flows identically before and after rotation; airfoil rotates but shows no aerodynamic influence on flow (e.g., no deflection, no stagnation line formation, no separation onset); flow remains perfectly straight and uniform across entire frame regardless of airfoil angle.
scc_specification.level_2: Smoke lines exist but show no causal relationship to airfoil: either they pass through the airfoil as if transparent, or they deflect randomly/unpredictably; rotation produces no systematic change in smoke pattern; no discernible stagnation point or streamline curvature near leading edge even at higher angles.
scc_specification.level_3: Smoke lines are visibly bent around the airfoil surface as rotation progresses; upstream lines remain straight and parallel; near the leading edge, lines converge and curve smoothly around the upper/lower surfaces; no flow reversal or separation bubble is required at this level, but curvature must be continuous and symmetric for low angles.
scc_specification.level_4: All elements of 3-score are present, AND as rotation continues, smoke lines increasingly diverge above and below the airfoil; upper-surface lines accelerate and arch upward, lower-surface lines decelerate and compress; a distinct stagnation point forms near the leading edge and migrates slightly downward as angle increases; no unphysical phenomena (e.g., smoke vanishing, splitting into discrete particles mid-stream, abrupt kinks unrelated to geometry).
scc_specification.level_5: All elements of 4-score are present, AND smoke lines demonstrate progressive distortion correlating with angle increase: at low angles, slight symmetric curvature; at moderate angles, asymmetric bending (stronger upper-surface deflection, lower-surface compression); no smoke line intersects or penetrates the airfoil surface; all lines remain continuous, unbroken, and attached (no detached vortices or turbulent shedding depicted, as those require unsteady conditions contrary to prompt).

Experimental Procedure
1. Add fluorophore-labeled anti-B-cell antibody to cell suspension tube.
2. Gently mix by swirling.

4. Wash cells by centrifugation and buffer resuspension.
5. Observe under fluorescence microscope or flow cytometer.

Fluorescent signal appears exclusively on intact, round B lymphocytes — no signal on debris or background; signal is bright, punctate, and membrane-localized.

B lymphocytes express surface immunoglobulins (e.g., CD19, CD20); fluorophore-conjugated antibodies bind specifically to these markers; after washing, only bound antibody remains, enabling detection via fluorescence.

subject: Human Physiology
selected_point: Blink reflex induced by a sudden puff of air near the eye
posted_prompt: A person is facing the camera, with one hand holding a bag and delivering a brief puff of air near one eye from the side.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Bilateral (consensual) corneal blink reflex elicited by a non-noxious air-puff stimulus delivered near one eye; because the trigeminal sensory signal is relayed to both facial motor nuclei in the brainstem, both eyes close together even though only one eye receives the stimulus.
Minimum mechanism: Intact trigeminal afferent pathway (V1) on the stimulated side, a bilateral brainstem relay, and an intact facial efferent pathway (CN VII) on both sides; the stimulus must be delivered to the cornea or periocular region of one eye, not a distant site; both eyelids must close, with the stimulated eye's closure occurring no later than the other eye's.
(ii)Storyline: [Phase 1] Person faces camera, both eyes open, hand holding bag at rest beside body. [Phase 2] Hand transports bag laterally into frame adjacent to one eye (same horizontal plane, no vertical offset). [Phase 3] Bag releases a puff (visually indicated by a subtle air disturbance or hand motion cue), immediately followed by rapid, full closure of both eyelids (a consensual blink), with the stimulated eye closing at the same moment as, or a fraction of a second before, the other eye. [Phase 4] Both eyes' eyelids reopen fully within the same sequence. [Visibility constraints] Both eyes must remain fully visible before, during, and after the blink; the bag and hand must not occlude either eye at stimulus onset; the viewpoint must remain fixed and frontal to capture the lateral stimulus delivery on one side and the bilateral (consensual) eyelid response on both sides.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Person faces the camera directly, stationary.
2. One hand holds a bag at waist or chest level.
3. The hand moves the bag laterally from the side (not the front) toward one eye, delivering a brief puff of air near it.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
Both eyes exhibit a rapid, complete, involuntary blink: all four eyelids (upper and lower, on both sides) close fully and nearly simultaneously, then reopen together. The eye nearer the puff may close a fraction of a second before the other eye, but the reflex does not produce a lone one-eyed closure while the other eye stays open.
Summary of Experimental Principles
The corneal blink reflex is a protective brainstem-mediated response: mechanical stimulation of the trigeminal nerve (V1 ophthalmic branch) on one side is relayed bilaterally to the facial motor nuclei (CN VII) in the pons, so orbicularis oculi contraction and eyelid closure occur on both sides even though the stimulus itself was delivered to only one eye.

subject: Digestive Physiology
selected_point: Amylase Activity Assay (Starch-Iodine Method)
posted_prompt: Place the starch solution into two test tubes separately. Add fresh saliva to one test tube and distilled water to the other. Let both test tubes stand undisturbed for a short period. Then add iodine solution drop by drop to both test tubes. Demonstrate the clear and simple hand operations using test tubes and pipettes.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Enzymatic hydrolysis of starch by salivary α-amylase, visualized via iodine complex disruption.
Minimum mechanism: Starch must be present in both tubes initially; amylase must be present *only* in saliva; iodine must be added *after* enzymatic reaction period; iodine-starch complex formation requires intact helical starch structure.
(ii)Storyline: Frame 1–2: Two empty test tubes enter view, fixed side-by-side. Frame 3–4: Pipette draws liquid from labeled saliva container → deposits into left tube. Frame 5–6: Pipette draws liquid from labeled distilled water container → deposits into right tube. Frame 7: Brief pause (no action, no movement) implying incubation. Frame 8–9: Iodine dropper approaches left tube → releases 2–3 discrete droplets → liquid color changes to pale yellow/amber. Frame 10: Iodine dropper approaches right tube → releases 2–3 discrete droplets → liquid color changes to or remains deep blue-black. All actions occur from fixed frontal viewpoint; no object leaves frame; liquid surfaces fully visible during all color observations.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place two identical transparent test tubes side-by-side.
2. Using a clean pipette, add fresh saliva to the first tube.
3. Using a clean pipette, add distilled water to the second tube.
4. Let both tubes stand undisturbed briefly, giving the enzyme time to act before iodine is added.
5. Add iodine solution drop-by-drop to both tubes.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
The tube with saliva becomes pale yellow/amber/colorless; the tube with distilled water remains deep blue-black.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Salivary amylase hydrolyzes starch into maltose, destroying the starch-iodine complex; intact starch binds iodine to produce blue-black color.

subject: Pharmacy
selected_point: Solubility of Crystalline and Amorphous Sugar Glasses in Water
posted_prompt: Two identical transparent beakers containing equal volumes of room temperature water are placed side by side; the beaker on the left is added with crystalline sugar, and the beaker on the right is added with sugar glass fragments, both being stirred gently with the same force.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Differential aqueous interaction kinetics between crystalline and amorphous sugar solids due to structural energy differences.
Minimum mechanism: Sugar glass must retain physical integrity long enough to be identifiable as fragments at t=0, then undergo visibly rapid dissolution (edges softening, shards fracturing, and fine cloudy material dispersing into the water), driven by its higher free energy and disordered structure; crystalline sugar, despite being intrinsically highly water-soluble, must dissolve far more slowly under the same brief stirring, so its grains stay visibly intact and largely undissolved over the observed timescale.
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0–1] Static wide shot: two identical beakers side-by-side, filled equally with clear water, empty except for labeled positions. [Frame 2–3] Crystalline sugar poured into left beaker (granular fall, settling with audible impact implied by visual particle bounce); sugar glass fragments dropped into right beaker (shard-like impact, minor splash, fragments rest visibly jagged). [Frame 4–7] Identical stirring tools enter both beakers synchronously; motion induces gentle vortex in both; left: sugar particles rotate but retain shape and separation; right: fragments wobble, chip at edges, release fine particulates causing localized cloudiness. [Frame 8–10] Stirring ceases; left beaker returns to still clarity with intact grains; right beaker shows persistent turbidity and suspended micro-fragments near bottom/sides. Fixed frontal viewpoint; full beaker height always visible; no occlusion; lighting uniform and diffuse.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place two identical transparent beakers side-by-side, each filled with equal volume of room temperature water.
2. Add crystalline sugar to left beaker; add sugar glass fragments to right beaker.
3. Simultaneously stir both beakers gently with identical tools using same motion.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
Crystalline sugar remains visibly granular and undissolved; sugar glass fragments rapidly fragment, cloud the water, and may form transient surface film — no full dissolution observed in 10 seconds.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Crystalline sucrose is actually highly water-soluble (on the order of 2 kg per liter of water at room temperature) — its ordered crystal lattice does not make it "low solubility," it makes dissolution slow, so under brief, gentle stirring the grains stay visibly intact within the short observed time window. Amorphous sugar glass has no long-range crystalline order and higher internal free energy, so it hydrates and breaks down much faster under the same conditions: fragments crack, soften, and shed fine, cloudy amorphous material into the water. The contrast in this clip reflects a difference in dissolution rate (kinetics), not a difference in whether the sugar is capable of dissolving.

posted_prompt: Two identical transparent beakers are placed side by side, each containing still distilled water; at the same time, liposome-encapsulated blue dye is added to the left beaker, and free blue dye is added to the right beaker.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Diffusion kinetics difference due to molecular confinement.
Minimum mechanism: Liposomes must remain structurally intact in water (no premature rupture), and free dye must be fully soluble and non-aggregating; water must be quiescent (no convection) to isolate diffusion-driven transport.
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0–1] Static wide shot showing two identical beakers with clear, still water; [Frame 2–3] Dropper tips enter frame simultaneously from top, aligned vertically over left/right beaker centers; [Frame 4] Identical blue droplets detach and contact water surfaces, causing symmetric transient dimples; [Frame 5–9] Free dye cloud expands radially with smooth intensity gradient; liposome-encapsulated dye retains compact, high-saturation shape with sharp boundaries; [Frame 10] Contrast in spread extent is maximally visible: free dye occupies ≥3× the area of liposome-encapsulated dye. Perspective: Fixed frontal orthographic view, centered on symmetry axis, no occlusion, full beaker height visible.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place two identical transparent beakers side-by-side on a flat surface, each filled with still distilled water.
2. Simultaneously add liposome-encapsulated blue dye to the left beaker and free blue dye to the right beaker.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
Free blue dye rapidly diffuses outward from entry point, forming an expanding, radially graded blue cloud. Liposome-encapsulated blue dye remains tightly localized near entry point with minimal outward spread and uniform internal color density.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Liposome encapsulation impedes passive diffusion by acting as a physical barrier; free dye molecules diffuse freely via Brownian motion, resulting in faster and broader dispersion in aqueous medium.
