subject: Pharmaceutical Chemistry
selected_point: Identification of Erythromycin Drugs (Sulfuric Acid Colorimetric Method)
posted_prompt: Transfer an appropriate amount of erythromycin reagent solution into a test tube. Slowly add concentrated sulfuric acid along the inner wall of the test tube using a pipette. Keep the test tube upright, gently shake to mix the contents, and observe the progress of the reaction inside the test tube.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Acid-induced chromogenic reaction of erythromycin in concentrated sulfuric acid, requiring interfacial contact, controlled mixing, and time-resolved color development.
Minimum mechanism: Erythromycin must be dissolved in aqueous medium; concentrated H₂SO₄ is fully miscible with the aqueous solution in all proportions but is much denser, so when it is added slowly along the tube wall it sinks and briefly forms a distinct lower layer rather than mixing instantly; reaction initiates at the acid–solution interface due to localized protonation/dehydration of erythromycin; color formation is diffusion-limited before shaking and requires mechanical agitation for homogenization.
(ii)Storyline: Frame 1–2: Upright empty test tube → Frame 3–4: Erythromycin solution added → Frame 5–6: Pipette contacts inner wall, acid begins flowing down → Frame 7: Distinct biphasic layering (upper aqueous, lower acid) visible → Frame 8: Reddish-brown band appears sharply at interface → Frame 9: Gentle shaking initiates → Frame 10: Color disperses upward continuously; final state is homogeneous reddish-brown. All events occur from fixed frontal viewpoint; tube remains fully in frame; no occlusion of interface or reaction zone; lighting remains constant to ensure visibility of color progression.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place a clean, dry test tube upright on bench.
2. Transfer erythromycin reagent solution into the tube (~1 mL).
3. Using a pipette, slowly dispense concentrated sulfuric acid along the inner wall of the tube.
4. Keep tube upright; gently shake to mix.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
A reddish-brown or cherry-red color develops first at the acid–aqueous interface, then disperses upward during shaking to yield a uniform reddish-brown solution. No precipitate or gas forms.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Erythromycin undergoes dehydration and rearrangement in concentrated H₂SO₄, forming chromophoric compounds that absorb visible light in the red-orange region — basis of the sulfuric acid colorimetric identification method.

pg_specification.level_1: No test tube present; no erythromycin reagent solution visible; no concentrated sulfuric acid container or pipette shown; no upright tube posture; no shaking action; no observable reaction zone.
pg_specification.level_2: Test tube is present and upright, but no liquid is identifiable as the erythromycin reagent solution (e.g., the tube is empty, or a liquid is shown with no source container, label, or addition action linking it to the reagent); concentrated sulfuric acid container or pipette is missing; no acid addition action shown; no mixing or shaking action depicted.
pg_specification.level_3: Test tube is present and upright; a liquid identifiable as the erythromycin reagent solution is present inside the tube, its identity established by context (e.g., poured from a labeled reagent bottle, or dispensed via a marked dropper) even if the liquid itself is colorless; concentrated sulfuric acid container and pipette are present; acid addition action is shown along the inner wall of the tube; shaking action is depicted; but no clear visual separation between layers, or no color develops at the interface.
pg_specification.level_4: All prompt-specified objects are present and correctly typed: test tube, erythromycin reagent solution (identifiable from context even if colorless), concentrated sulfuric acid container, pipette; acid addition occurs along the inner wall while the tube remains upright; gentle shaking is shown; a layered appearance (upper aqueous phase, lower denser acid phase) is visible before shaking.
pg_specification.level_5: All elements in score 4 are present AND the acid addition is delivered exclusively along the inner wall (no splashing, no dripping outside the wall, no direct drop into the bulk liquid); the tube remains upright throughout addition and shaking; the shaking motion shown is gentle and brief (no vigorous swirling or full inversion of the tube); the liquid volume visibly matches what was added, with no unexplained spillage or overflow; no extraneous tools or containers beyond the pipette, acid container, and test tube appear in frame.

subject: Skin Physiology
selected_point: Erythema reaction (friction)
posted_prompt: A clean forearm is displayed. A hand with a smooth pad rubs the same skin area back and forth with moderate force for several seconds, then stops, and the skin is left exposed for observation.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Friction-induced erythema as a transient, localized, vascular physiological response.
Minimum mechanism: Mechanical shear stress on epidermis must trigger neurogenic and endothelial-mediated arteriolar dilation in the dermal plexus, resulting in increased perfusion and hemoglobin-dependent redness, requiring intact microvasculature, normal autonomic tone, and absence of vasoconstrictive agents.
(ii)Storyline: [Phase 1: Baseline] Clean forearm fully visible, static, evenly lit, no redness. [Phase 2: Intervention] Hand enters frame holding smooth pad; pad contacts skin; back-and-forth linear motion begins on fixed locus; motion is continuous, planar, and confined. [Phase 3: Cessation] Motion stops abruptly; hand either lifts cleanly or holds pad stationary without pressure; no repositioning. [Phase 4: Observation] Skin remains fully exposed, motionless, and uniformly lit for ≥2 seconds; erythema emerges *only* in rubbed zone, with homogeneous pink-to-red hue, sharp spatial boundaries matching pad contact area, and no fading during observation. Perspective: Fixed frontal close-up (elbow to wrist), no camera movement, no occlusion, consistent focal plane throughout.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Display a clean, bare forearm centered in frame.
2. A hand holding a smooth, matte pad contacts the forearm skin.
3. Rub the same skin area back and forth with moderate, steady pressure for several seconds.
4. Stop rubbing completely and withdraw hand slightly while keeping pad in place or lifting cleanly.
5. Leave skin fully exposed and motionless for observation.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
A localized, homogeneous pink-to-red erythematous area appears exclusively within the rubbed region after rubbing ceases and persists during observation; no swelling, blistering, or discoloration outside this zone.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Erythema reaction is a transient, friction-induced vasodilation of superficial capillaries; it manifests as reversible, localized reddening due to increased blood flow and capillary engorgement — a normal physiological response to mechanical stimulation of healthy skin.

pg_specification.level_1: No forearm is shown, or no hand/pad rubbing action occurs, or the skin is never left exposed for observation after rubbing: at least one of the three stages (clean forearm, rubbing, post-rub observation) is missing entirely.
pg_specification.level_2: The forearm shown has visible hair, jewelry, or clothing covering part of the skin; the hand is present but is not holding anything resembling a smooth pad (e.g., bare fingers only, or a clearly textured/rough object); the motion shown is tapping, pressing, or single-direction wiping rather than a repeated back-and-forth rub; the video ends before any post-rub still-exposure period.
pg_specification.level_3: A bare forearm is shown, a hand holding a smooth pad contacts the skin and rubs back and forth for several seconds over the same spot, the rubbing stops, and the skin is then left visible and still: all three stages occur in the correct order, though the pad's texture or the forearm's starting condition may not perfectly match the prompt (e.g., the pad looks slightly textured, or the forearm already had a mark before rubbing).
pg_specification.level_4: Everything in the 3-point level holds, and in addition the pad is smooth and matte with no obvious texture or pattern, the forearm is bare with no gloves, sleeves, or digital overlays, no extra hands or objects enter the frame, and the rubbing stays confined to one patch of skin rather than drifting across the arm.

scc_specification.level_1: No pink or red mark ever appears on the skin, or the skin's color never changes from its starting tone, or a color change appears with no connection to where the rubbing happened.
scc_specification.level_2: A red or pink mark appears somewhere other than the rubbed patch (e.g., on the palm, surrounding skin, or in the background); or the mark appears before rubbing starts; or the mark visibly fades away while rubbing is still happening; or the color that appears is not a plausible skin-reddening tone (e.g., purple, yellow, or blue).

subject: Skin Physiology
selected_point: Dermatographism (Delayed Type)
posted_prompt: Demonstrate delayed dermographism. Select the forearm of a healthy adult for the procedure. Use a blunt stick to draw a straight line on the skin with moderate pressure. After an interval representing the multi-hour delay characteristic of this reaction (shown here in compressed form), re-examine the marked area. Clearly demonstrate the entire procedure step by step.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Delayed dermographism as a mast-cell–mediated cutaneous hypersensitivity response to mechanical trauma.
Minimum mechanism: Mechanical pressure must trigger delayed (not immediate) histamine release causing localized capillary leak and dermal edema, requiring intact mast cells, functional histamine receptors, and normal vascular permeability; absence of concurrent urticaria or systemic illness.
(ii)Storyline: Phase 1 (Baseline): Static shot of healthy volar forearm under diffuse lighting: skin smooth, uniform pink-red tone, no lesions. Phase 2 (Stimulation): Blunt stick enters frame, contacts skin, and draws straight line with visible transient blanching/indentation, no wheal. Phase 3 (Latency): Absolute stillness, same frame, same lighting, no skin change. Phase 4 (Reaction): At re-examination onset, linear wheal emerges *de novo* along drawn path: continuous, elevated, homogeneously pink-red, coextensive with line, no spread beyond margins. Visibility constraints: Fixed frontal view; no occlusion; full focus on skin surface; lighting reveals subtle elevation and color contrast against baseline.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Position volar forearm of healthy adult in stable, well-lit view.
2. Use blunt, rounded-tip stick to draw one straight line on skin with moderate pressure.
3. Pause — this stands in for the multi-hour real-world latency period; maintain visible stillness for the shown interval.
4. Re-examine the exact same skin location.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
A delayed, linear, raised, pink-to-red wheal appears exclusively along the path of the prior line during re-examination — absent during drawing and pause.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Delayed dermographism is a variant of skin hypersensitivity in which mechanical stimulation triggers mast cell degranulation only after a lag period — classically 3–8 hours, with wheals that can persist up to 48 hours — resulting in localized histamine-mediated wheal formation along the line of pressure. This is distinct from immediate (simple) dermographism, in which the wheal appears within minutes of stimulation.

pg_specification.level_2: The forearm is visible and correctly oriented, but at least two of the three required steps are missing or wrong: e.g., the tool used is a pointed object (needle, fingernail, stylus) instead of a blunt stick, or no linear drawing motion is shown (just pressing), or the re-examination shot is missing entirely.
pg_specification.level_3: All three steps appear in order: (1) a blunt stick contacts the forearm and moves in a line to draw a straight mark, (2) a visible pause follows with no further marking, (3) the camera returns to the forearm to show the marked area; but at least one execution flaw remains: the line is visibly not straight, or the re-examination view is clearly a different patch of skin than where the line was drawn, or the stick's tip looks pointed rather than blunt.
pg_specification.level_4: All three steps appear in correct order and are spatially faithful: a stick with a clearly rounded, non-pointed tip draws one continuous straight line on the forearm; an unbroken pause follows with no drawing motion or camera movement; the re-examination shot shows the same patch of skin, same orientation, same framing; but one visual detail is off: the drawing shows no visible skin indentation/blanching from pressure, or the re-examination shot is soft-focus, partly blocked, or reframed compared to the drawing shot.

subject: Nutrition & Dietetics
selected_point: Milk protein denaturation caused by acid and formation of curd
posted_prompt: In a transparent glass bowl containing warm milk, slowly add vinegar while gently stirring with a spoon.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Acid-induced protein denaturation and aggregation into visible curds in warm dairy matrix.
Minimum mechanism: Vinegar (acetic acid) must contact warm milk; acid protons disrupt casein micelle stability; denatured proteins coalesce into insoluble aggregates large enough to scatter light and appear as opaque white curds; separation from whey requires sufficient aggregation and reduced solubility.
(ii)Storyline: Frame 0–2: Static shot of a transparent glass bowl holding uniform warm milk (subtle surface sheen, no chill cue). Frame 3–5: A spoon enters the milk and begins a slow, continuous circular stir. Frame 6–8: While the spoon keeps circulating, vinegar is poured in a thin stream from a container held above the bowl, landing in the region the spoon is stirring; curds begin appearing within that stirred zone as opaque white clusters. Frame 9–10: Curds persist and grow in number/size as stirring continues; a clear contrast is visible between curds (opaque, granular, solid-like) and the surrounding whey (translucent, smoother, less opaque), with the bowl, milk, vinegar source, and spoon all held in the same frontal/slightly-angled framing throughout.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place warm milk in a transparent glass bowl.
2. Slowly add vinegar into the bowl while gently stirring with a spoon.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
White curds form and separate from translucent whey as vinegar mixes into warm milk; curds appear as opaque, grainy, lump-like clusters suspended in liquid.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Acid (vinegar) denatures milk proteins (e.g., casein), causing them to unfold and aggregate into solid curds; warmth accelerates this process.

pg_specification.level_1: No transparent glass bowl is shown; no milk (warm or otherwise) is visible in it; no vinegar container or vinegar stream appears anywhere; no spoon is present; nothing resembling this milk-and-vinegar curdling setup appears at any point.
pg_specification.level_2: A transparent glass bowl holding a white liquid is shown, but the liquid does not read as warm milk (no surface sheen or any warmth cue; it could pass for a cold liquid or something else entirely); and/or no vinegar container or stream is ever shown near the bowl; a spoon may be present but never touches the liquid, and no pouring or stirring action occurs.
pg_specification.level_3: The bowl holds a milk-like white liquid, a container tips and releases a visible stream into the bowl (readable as the vinegar addition), and a spoon dips into and moves through the liquid at some point; but the setup fails to line up as one coherent action: e.g., the vinegar is poured in completely before the spoon ever enters and starts moving (no overlap between the pour and the stir), or the vinegar container and the bowl appear in separate shots or mismatched camera angles rather than together in one frame.
pg_specification.level_4: The bowl holds warm milk with a visible surface sheen; a spoon enters the bowl first and begins a slow, continuous circular stir; while the spoon keeps moving, a container tips above the bowl rim and a visible vinegar stream enters the milk; the bowl, milk, vinegar container, and spoon stay in one fixed side-by-side arrangement under one consistent camera framing for the whole sequence, matching the manual's order: milk already in the bowl, then vinegar added while stirring is already underway.
pg_specification.level_5: All elements of score 4 are satisfied, and additionally: the spoon's circular stirring is already running before the first vinegar drop lands and keeps going without pause through the entire pour, rather than starting only once the pour is finished; the vinegar stream visibly lands in the same patch of milk the spoon is actively moving through, rather than in an untouched corner of the bowl; the framing keeps the bowl rim, milk surface, spoon handle, and vinegar container all legible together at the exact moment the vinegar starts entering the milk.

scc_specification.level_1: No state change is observed anywhere in the bowl: the milk stays a uniform, fully liquid white from start to finish; no curds, no cloudiness, and no change in opacity ever appear, even after the vinegar reaches the milk.
scc_specification.level_2: The milk grows slightly cloudier or thicker-looking after the vinegar reaches it, but no discrete curd particles ever form; there is no visible separation between solid curd and liquid whey, and the overall color/opacity change looks the same everywhere in the bowl regardless of where the vinegar or spoon has been, giving no visual link between the vinegar addition and the change.
scc_specification.level_3: After the vinegar reaches the milk, a patch of cloudiness or faint opacity appears, but it never resolves into distinct curd particles (no grainy or lumpy texture is visible); no separation between solid curd and clear whey is shown; the milk's color stays white while overall clarity drops unevenly, but the change looks delayed, patchy, or unrelated to where the vinegar entered or the spoon has stirred.
scc_specification.level_4: Distinct white curd clumps appear within the milk after the vinegar reaches it; each clump is visually distinguishable from the surrounding milk by its lumpy/grainy shape, its rougher texture, and its greater opacity; curds appear only after vinegar has entered the bowl and only in the area the spoon has stirred it into, with no curd visible anywhere beforehand.
scc_specification.level_5: All elements of score 4 are satisfied, and additionally: the curd clumps keep growing in size and number as stirring continues after the vinegar is added; they stay suspended in the liquid rather than fully sinking or dissolving back into a smooth liquid; a visibly clearer, less opaque whey appears around the curds, so the opaque curd clusters and the more translucent whey remain clearly distinguishable from each other for the rest of the stirring.

sc_specification.level_1: The spoon or the vinegar stream jumps into the shot with no entry motion (e.g., the spoon is suddenly inside the milk with no hand or handle bringing it in); the glass bowl's position or tilt changes abruptly between frames with no hand or force shown moving it; the reflection of the room's light on the milk surface switches from one side of the bowl to the other with no visible cause; the milk surface ripples in physically impossible ways (e.g., ripples spreading from an empty patch, or freezing into a rigid pattern); the bowl rim visibly breaks apart or vanishes for part of the video.
sc_specification.level_2: The spoon enters the bowl with a visibly broken path (e.g., it is outside the bowl in one frame and already submerged in the next, skipping the entry motion); the vinegar stream appears mid-air already fully formed rather than emerging from the container's spout; the reflected highlight on the milk's surface stays fixed in place even as the spoon disturbs the surface; a short freeze or a duplicated-frame stutter occurs, or the room lighting flickers once for no reason tied to the action.

subject: Nutrition & Dietetics
selected_point: Frozen and thawed strawberries exhibit ice crystal textural damage
posted_prompt: Freeze whole strawberries and thaw them at room temperature; show a close-up image of the thawed strawberries being gently pressed or cut open.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Ice crystal-mediated cellular rupture during freeze-thaw cycle in fleshy fruit tissue.
Minimum mechanism: Extracellular ice nucleation must occur during freezing, generating mechanical stress that breaches plasma membranes; upon thawing, loss of turgor and cytoplasmic leakage must manifest as irreversible softening, skin failure, and juice exudation, all visually observable without instrumentation.
(ii)Storyline: [Phase 1: Baseline] Fresh whole strawberries shown intact, firm, dry-skinned, with defined seeds and uniform red hue. [Phase 2: Freezing] Visible frost accumulation or freezer insertion confirming phase change; strawberries become rigid and opaque. [Phase 3: Thawing] Surface moisture appears, ambient context confirms room temperature, berries visibly slump/sag. [Phase 4: Close-up + Intervention] Stable macro view holds thawed berry; either (a) fingertip contact induces immediate, non-recovering surface depression with lateral skin stretching, OR (b) knife blade enters cleanly and cut exposes disintegrated pulp with free liquid pooling at interface. Experimental Procedure
1. Place fresh whole strawberries on a clean surface.

3. Remove and allow to thaw completely at room temperature.

5. Gently press one strawberry with fingertip OR cut one open with a knife.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
Thawed strawberries show irreversible softening: surface indents permanently under light pressure; skin splits or tears easily; cutting reveals waterlogged, fragmented interior with immediate juice leakage.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Freezing forms extracellular ice crystals that puncture cell membranes; thawing releases intracellular water, causing structural collapse and textural damage — characteristic of frozen-thawed whole berries.

subject: Physics
selected_point: Moving a bar magnet back and forth within a copper wire coil connected to a galvanometer
posted_prompt: A bar magnet is pushed into and pulled out of a copper wire coil connected to a galvanometer, whose needle is clearly visible.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Electromagnetic induction via relative motion between a permanent magnet and a closed copper coil, producing transient current detectable by galvanometer deflection.
Minimum mechanism: Coil must be electrically closed (no breaks), made of conductive copper (not aluminum/steel), wound as a multi-turn helix; magnet must have dipole field (bar shape); galvanometer must be analog, center-zero, and sensitive to microcurrents; motion must change magnetic flux linkage through coil area.
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0–t1] Static setup: bar magnet held near but outside coil entrance, galvanometer needle at zero; [t1–t2] Magnet moves coaxially into coil → needle deflects steadily in one direction; [t2–t3] Magnet stops fully inside → needle returns smoothly toward zero; [t3–t4] Magnet moves coaxially out of coil → needle deflects steadily in opposite direction; [t4–end] Magnet fully withdrawn → needle returns to zero. Entire sequence must be captured in single fixed-viewpoint shot with all three objects continuously visible and spatially coherent.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Hold a bar magnet horizontally and align it with the central axis of a stationary copper wire coil.
2. Push the magnet steadily into the coil until fully inserted.
3. Pull the magnet steadily back out of the coil.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
The galvanometer needle deflects in one direction when the magnet is pushed in, returns toward zero when motion stops, then deflects in the opposite direction when the magnet is pulled out.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Relative motion between a magnetic field and a closed conductive loop induces an electromotive force (EMF), causing current flow; direction of induced current follows Lenz’s law — opposing the change in magnetic flux.

subject: Physics
selected_point: The zinc plate on the electroscope, when exposed to ultraviolet light, causes discharge.
posted_prompt: A negatively charged gold-leaf electroscope, equipped with a zinc plate at its top, is illuminated by a lamp that alternately emits light in the visible and ultraviolet ranges at the same distance.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Photoelectric discharge of a negatively charged electroscope via UV-induced electron emission from zinc.
Minimum mechanism: Zinc must be present and illuminated; UV photons must exceed zinc's work function (~4.3 eV, wavelength below ~290 nm); emitted electrons carry away negative charge, reducing leaf repulsion; this charge loss is not restored by subsequent visible-light exposure, since visible photons (wavelength above ~400 nm) lack the energy to eject electrons or add charge back; leaves respond to UV exposure with convergence that persists once the light source returns to the visible range.
(ii)Storyline: Frame 0–2s: Stable shot of diverged gold leaves under visible light; zinc plate clearly attached, lamp emits warm/white light. Frame 2–4s: Lamp visibly switches mode (e.g., glow shifts to violet, filter rotates in, or icon changes); leaves begin smooth, continuous convergence. Frame 4–6s: UV mode sustained; leaves reach a fully converged (or maximally converged) position. Frame 6–8s: Lamp switches back to visible mode; the converged leaf position holds steady, since the charge carried away during UV exposure is not restored by visible light. Frame 8–10s: Visible mode sustained; leaves remain at their converged position, confirming that only UV, not visible light, altered the electroscope's charge. Throughout: Fixed viewpoint, no occlusion, no external intervention, no lighting discontinuity.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place a negatively charged gold-leaf electroscope with zinc plate mounted on top.
2. Position a lamp at fixed distance, emitting visible light first.
3. Switch lamp to ultraviolet emission mode.
4. Observe gold-leaf behavior across both modes.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
During visible light: gold leaves remain diverged.
During ultraviolet light: gold leaves gradually collapse (converge).
Summary of Experimental Principles
Ultraviolet light causes photoelectric emission from the zinc plate, discharging the electroscope; visible light lacks sufficient photon energy to eject electrons, so no discharge occurs.

subject: Chemistry
selected_point: Adding dish soap to an oil–water mixture forms a stable emulsion.
posted_prompt: Place two identical jars side by side, each containing water and a layer of oil; add dish soap only to the right jar, seal both jars, and shake them vigorously.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Surfactant-mediated stabilization of oil-in-water emulsions.
Minimum mechanism: Oil and water are immiscible; without surfactant, dispersed droplets coalesce rapidly upon agitation cessation; with surfactant (dish soap), droplets remain sterically and electrostatically stabilized against coalescence, yielding persistent macroscopic homogeneity.
(ii)Storyline: [Phase 1: Baseline] Two identical jars side-by-side, each showing quiescent, sharply layered water (bottom) and oil (top); [Phase 2: Intervention] Dish soap introduced exclusively into right jar (visible droplet entry), then both jars sealed (lids fully covering openings); [Phase 3: Action] Both jars undergo synchronous, vigorous shaking: liquid inside surges, mixes, and becomes temporarily turbid; [Phase 4: Outcome] Jars held still: left jar clears completely into two distinct layers within seconds; right jar retains uniform, featureless cloudiness with no interface or settling, all observed from fixed frontal viewpoint with no occlusion or framing shift.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place two identical transparent jars side-by-side; fill each with equal volumes of water (bottom layer) and oil (top layer).
2. Add dish soap only to the right jar.
3. Seal both jars with lids.
4. Shake both jars vigorously and simultaneously.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
After shaking stops and jars are held still: left jar rapidly reseparates into two sharp layers; right jar remains uniformly cloudy/milky with no layering — a stable emulsion.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Dish soap acts as a surfactant, reducing interfacial tension between oil and water, enabling oil to disperse into tiny droplets stabilized by soap micelles — forming a stable emulsion.

subject: Chemistry
selected_point: The Reaction of Iodine with Starch Compared to Cellulose (Effects of Polymer Structure on Binding)
posted_prompt: Two transparent beakers are placed side by side: one contains a starch suspension, and the other contains cellulose fibers; iodine solution is added to both.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Differential iodine-induced coloration due to structural complementarity between iodine and amylose helices versus absence thereof in cellulose.
Minimum mechanism: Iodine must physically contact starch to trigger blue-black complex formation; cellulose must remain physically distinct (non-dissolved, non-gelatinized) and structurally inert to iodine under ambient conditions.
(ii)Storyline: Frame 0–2: Static shot revealing two side-by-side transparent beakers: left contains cloudy starch suspension, right contains discrete cellulose fibers; no iodine yet. Frame 3–5: Iodine solution visibly dispensed into left beaker → immediate, uniform blue-black color development confined within suspension. Frame 6–8: Iodine solution dispensed into right beaker → no color change; fibers retain original appearance and texture. Frame 9–10: Final stable contrast held (blue-black starch vs. unchanged cellulose) under consistent lighting and fixed viewpoint. Visibility constraint: Entire beaker bodies, liquid/fiber interfaces, and iodine contact zones must remain fully in-frame and unoccluded at all times; no cutaways, inserts, or text overlays.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place two transparent beakers side-by-side on a neutral background.
2. Fill left beaker with starch suspension (opaque white/cloudy liquid).
3. Fill right beaker with cellulose fibers (dry, fibrous, off-white solid).
4. Add iodine solution (amber/brown liquid) to both beakers simultaneously or sequentially.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
- Starch suspension turns instantly blue-black upon iodine contact.
- Cellulose fibers show no color change — remain off-white/brown and fibrous.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Iodine forms polyhalide complexes with amylose helices in starch, producing blue-black color; cellulose lacks helical structure and does not bind iodine, so no color change occurs — demonstrating how polymer conformation dictates molecular binding.

(i) Target concept: Visual demonstration of sexual dimorphism via presence/absence of a species-typical morphological trait (bright iridescent, metallic-sheen plumage) tied to biological sex.
Minimum mechanism: The iridescent plumage patch is a fixed, non-behavioral, anatomically anchored feature of the male's feathers (e.g., on the throat, crown, or back); its absence in females, who show plain, dull, non-iridescent plumage, is complete and developmentally invariant, with no ontogenetic overlap or environmental modulation.
(ii)Storyline: Frame opens with a stable, front-facing, full-body view of two sunbirds aligned horizontally. Left bird is motionless, uniformly dull-toned (brown, olive, or gray), with no bright or metallic-sheen feather patch anywhere on its body. Right bird is motionless, with the same posture, but shows a bright, iridescent/metallic-sheen plumage patch clearly distinct from its own surrounding duller feathers. Perspective is frontal and orthogonal (no foreshortening), ensuring the presence/absence of iridescent plumage is legible without inference.

Experimental Procedure
1. Display two African sunbirds side-by-side in the same static frame: female on left, male on right.

2. Female shows plain, dull brown or olive-gray plumage with no iridescent sheen; male shows a bright, iridescent, metallic-colored plumage patch (e.g., on throat, crown, or back) that contrasts with his own duller feathers and with the female's plumage.
Summary of Experimental Principles
3. Sexual dimorphism in African sunbirds: males display bright iridescent/metallic plumage (e.g., on the throat, crown, or back) as a secondary sexual characteristic used in courtship display, while females display plain, non-iridescent plumage.

subject: Morphology
selected_point: Reverse sexual dimorphism in the woodpecker: females possess red crown feathers, whereas red crowns are typically found in males.
posted_prompt: Mark the sex of two woodpeckers. Use a pointing rod to indicate the color and morphological differences in the red crown feathers between males and females.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Visual identification of sex via crown color dimorphism in woodpeckers.
Minimum mechanism: Two conspecific woodpeckers must be co-present, statically posed, with crowns fully visible and lit to resolve spectral differences; rod must physically contact crown to establish referential link; color perception must support red vs. non-red discrimination without metamerism or display gamut failure.
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0–2] Stable wide shot reveals two woodpeckers side-by-side, heads upright, crowns fully in view. [Frame 3–4] Pointing rod enters frame from bottom, moves upward. [Frame 5–6] Rod tip contacts crown of left woodpecker: red color fully visible. [Frame 7–8] Rod tip lifts *without leaving frame*, moves laterally, contacts crown of right woodpecker: non-red color fully visible. [Frame 9–10] Rod remains in contact with second crown; both crowns stay in focus, unoccluded, and color-stable until end. Perspective: fixed frontal/slightly elevated viewpoint; no camera motion; no cutaways; all events occur within single continuous take.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place two live woodpeckers side-by-side in natural lighting.
2. Use a thin, neutral-colored pointing rod to touch the crown region of the first woodpecker, then the second.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
One woodpecker exhibits a fully red crown; the other exhibits a non-red (black/brown/gray) crown — no red pigment visible on the latter.
Summary of Experimental Principles
This species shows reverse sexual dimorphism: unlike most woodpeckers, where the red crown marks males, here the red crown marks the female, while the male shows the non-red (black/brown/gray) crown.

pg_specification.level_1: No two woodpeckers appear together in the frame (e.g., only one bird, or a single bird shown twice across a cut); or no pointing rod is ever visible; or neither bird's crown is ever shown; or the two woodpeckers are positioned one behind the other or diagonally rather than beside each other, so their crowns can't be compared in the same glance.
pg_specification.level_2: Two woodpeckers are shown beside each other, but the pointing rod never appears; or the rod appears but never touches either bird's crown; or the rod touches a crown but it is unclear which of the two birds is being indicated; or a crown is present but hidden by feathers, shadow, or the frame edge so its color can't be judged.
pg_specification.level_3: Two woodpeckers are shown beside each other; the pointing rod touches the crown of each bird in turn (or touches both at once); each bird's crown is plainly visible enough to judge its color; a viewer can tell, from the rod's position alone, which bird is being indicated at each moment, with no on-screen text or narration required.
pg_specification.level_4: Everything required at the 3-point level, plus: the rod stays in contact with a crown for the whole time it indicates that bird rather than tapping and lifting away repeatedly; the two woodpeckers stay in the same shot throughout, with no cut or re-framing between the two indications; the rod visibly moves from the first bird's crown to the second's (or holds both at once), so the labeling order is unambiguous; both birds show a woodpecker-typical head shape and chisel-like bill, with no oversized eyes, bare/featherless skin, or other non-avian features.
pg_specification.level_5: Everything required at the 4-point level, plus: the rod only ever touches the crown itself (never the nape, back, or cheek) of either bird; both woodpeckers face the camera closely enough that the whole crown is exposed and unobstructed; no hand, extra tool, or on-screen label enters the shot to block the view of either crown or confuse which bird the rod is touching.

subject: Biochemistry & Molecular Biology
selected_point: Thermophilic catalase produces oxygen bubbles after heat treatment, compared to n.
posted_prompt: Two adjacent transparent beakers: red heat-stable catalase and blue regular catalase are heated in a water bath, followed by the simultaneous addition of hydrogen peroxide.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Enzyme thermostability determines catalytic capacity under heat stress.
Minimum mechanism: Heat-stable catalase must remain folded and active post-heating to rapidly cleave H₂O₂ → O₂(g) + H₂O(l), while heat-labile catalase must be irreversibly denatured and inert under identical conditions.
(ii)Storyline: Frame 1–2: Static wide shot showing two adjacent beakers in water bath, red solution in left, blue in right. Frame 3–4: Water bath visibly quiescent, no steam or boiling, confirming controlled heating (not boiling). Frame 5: Dual dropper or synchronized twin application delivers H₂O₂ to both beaker surfaces in same instant. Frame 6–10: Immediate, exclusive bubble nucleation and ascent in red beaker; blue beaker surface remains optically flat and motionless: no effervescence, no meniscus disturbance, no micro-turbulence. Viewpoint remains fixed, frontal, and orthogonal to beaker row; no occlusion, no camera motion, no lighting shift.

Experimental Procedure
1. Place two identical transparent beakers side-by-side in a water bath.
2. Fill left beaker with red heat-stable catalase solution; fill right beaker with blue regular catalase solution.
3. Heat both beakers in water bath until thermal equilibrium reached.
4. Simultaneously add hydrogen peroxide to both beakers.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
Only the red beaker produces continuous, vigorous oxygen bubbles after hydrogen peroxide addition; the blue beaker shows no bubble formation.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Thermophilic catalase retains enzymatic activity after heat treatment and decomposes H₂O₂ into O₂ and H₂O, producing visible oxygen bubbles; regular catalase is denatured by heat and loses function, producing no bubbles.

subject: Biochemistry & Molecular Biology
selected_point: A simple laboratory demonstration: Fluorescent RNA products accumulate gradually in a test tube over time
posted_prompt: On an experimental bench, two test tubes with blue and red caps are present; a gloved hand adds DNA template, nucleotides, and RNA polymerase to the blue-capped tube, after which both tubes are placed under ultraviolet light.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: In vitro transcription-dependent fluorescent signal generation requires all three core reagents (DNA template, nucleotides, RNA polymerase) to be co-localized in a single reaction vessel; fluorescence is contingent on both successful enzymatic synthesis and subsequent UV excitation.
Minimum mechanism: RNA polymerase must bind DNA template and catalyze phosphodiester bond formation using nucleotides to produce RNA; fluorescent signal arises only from RNA-dye complexes (not free dye or reagents alone); UV illumination is necessary but insufficient without RNA product.
(ii)Storyline: Frame 1–3: Static side-by-side view of blue-capped and red-capped tubes on bench. Frame 4–6: Gloved hand enters frame, retrieves reagents, and delivers them exclusively into blue-capped tube (no contact with red tube). Frame 7–8: Both tubes remain stationary and unmoved. Frame 9–10: UV light activates: immediate onset of fluorescence exclusively in blue-capped tube, with visible progressive brightening; red-capped tube shows zero emission. All events occur from fixed frontal bench-level viewpoint; no camera movement; no occlusion of tubes or hand during critical actions.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place two upright test tubes side-by-side on bench: left tube has blue cap, right tube has red cap.
2. Using gloved hand, add DNA template, nucleotides, and RNA polymerase exclusively to blue-capped tube.
3. Place both tubes under ultraviolet light.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
Under UV light, only the blue-capped tube emits visible fluorescence; the red-capped tube remains non-fluorescent. Fluorescence appears gradually and intensifies over time within the blue-capped tube.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Fluorescent RNA products form only when transcription occurs: DNA template + nucleotides + RNA polymerase enable RNA synthesis. RNA binds fluorescent dye (inherent or co-administered), causing UV-induced fluorescence. No transcription components in red-capped tube → no RNA → no fluorescence.

subject: Ecology & Evolutionary Biology
selected_point: Courtship behavior of the European Robin: both sexes share the same orange-red breast (visually monomorphic), so courtship is signaled by behavior — males orient and present the breast while perched, and females respond with wing-quivering.
posted_prompt: A male robin perches on a branch, engaged in a courtship interaction with a female robin perched on an adjacent branch. Fixed camera position, natural outdoor lighting, continuous unedited recording, no narration or text overlay.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Sex-specific courtship BEHAVIOR in the European Robin (Erithacus rubecula). Note: both sexes of this species carry the same orange-red breast plumage (they are visually monomorphic), so the courtship exchange is distinguished by behavior, not color: the male stays perched and orients/presents his breast toward the female (no hovering display is required or expected; European Robin courtship display is perch-based); the female, also perched, responds with a bout of wing-quivering, a receptive/solicitation display related to courtship-feeding behavior in this species.
Minimum mechanism: the male's breast-presentation requires an unobstructed, camera-facing or oblique orientation and enough ambient light for the orange-red breast to register; the female's wing-quiver requires a stable perch and an unobstructed view of both wings; because the species is monomorphic, no color difference between the two birds should be scored as a criterion; only their perched positions, orientation, and distinct behaviors identify which bird is male and which is female.
(ii) Storyline: [Phase 1] Male perches stably on a branch, oriented toward the female → [Phase 2] Male presents his orange-red breast (frontal or oblique view, unoccluded), remaining perched throughout → [Phase 3] Female, perched on an adjacent branch, responds with a bout of bilateral wing-quivering → [Phase 4] Both birds maintain their perched positions and behavior for a sustained interval → Perspective constraint: fixed camera keeps both birds' full bodies visible, the male's breast oriented toward the camera-facing side, and wing-quivering fully visible in-plane; any foliage occlusion must be brief and natural only.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place a live male European robin on a natural branch in partial shade; place a live female European robin on an adjacent branch within the same line of sight.
2. Position a fixed camera at eye level, 2–3 m distance, capturing both birds in frame under natural daylight.
3. Record continuously for 10 seconds with no intervention.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
- The male robin remains perched throughout and orients his body to present his orange-red breast toward the female.
- The female robin remains perched throughout and performs a bout of bilateral wing-quivering, a receptive/solicitation display associated with courtship feeding in this species.
- Both birds maintain adjacent spatial relationship; no flight, hovering, aggression, or disengagement is observed.
Summary of Experimental Principles
European robins (Erithacus rubecula) are sexually monomorphic in plumage — both sexes carry the same orange-red breast — so sex-specific courtship roles are conveyed through behavior rather than coloration: the male perches and orients/presents his breast as a courtship display, while the female signals receptivity by wing-quivering while perched. Both behaviors are innate, sex-specific, and occur in close proximity under natural lighting; no hovering display is part of this mechanism.

subject: Cell & Developmental Biology
selected_point: Fluorescently labeled glucocorticoid receptors translocate from the cytoplasm to the nucleus.

Green fluorescence remains diffuse/cytoplasmic in right well cells; in left well cells, green signal progressively accumulates inside morphologically identifiable nuclei — nuclear regions become distinctly brighter than surrounding cytoplasm.

Fluorescently labeled glucocorticoid receptors translocate from the cytoplasm to the nucleus upon hormone binding.

subject: Cell & Developmental Biology
selected_point: After lysing the cell culture, centrifugation results in a pellet of cellular debris, with the clarified supernatant remaining above.
posted_prompt: A microcentrifuge tube containing cell culture lysate was removed from a benchtop centrifuge immediately after a complete high-speed spin and held upright, motionless, in hand.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: The state of a cell lysate inside a microcentrifuge tube immediately after a completed benchtop centrifugation run, once mechanical separation of debris from soluble material has finished.
Minimum mechanism: The centrifugal force applied during the spin must have already sedimented the denser cellular debris into a compact pellet at the tube's conical bottom, leaving the less dense soluble material as a comparatively clear supernatant above it; because the spin is complete before the tube is removed, this pellet and the clearer fluid above it are already present and stable at the moment the tube is lifted out and held still; nothing further needs to separate on screen.
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0] Tube sits in the centrifuge rotor with the rotor already stopped and the lid open; [Frame 1-3] a hand reaches in, grasps the tube, and lifts it straight up out of the rotor cavity; [Frame 4-10] the tube is held upright and motionless, revealing a denser mass settled at its conical bottom and a comparatively clear fluid layer above it, with the boundary between the two staying fixed as the tube is held still; no shaking, no re-mixing of the settled mass back into the fluid above; viewpoint stays fixed, frontal or slightly oblique, showing the tube's full length so the bottom mass and the fluid above it are both visible; lighting stays directional and steady enough to make out the boundary between them.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Centrifuge a lysed cell culture at high speed for the standard time needed to complete pelleting (a full clarifying spin, not a brief pulse).
2. Remove the microcentrifuge tube from the benchtop centrifuge once the rotor has fully stopped, and hold it upright, motionless.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
A compact, opaque mass of cellular debris sits at the tube's conical bottom, with a visible boundary separating it from the comparatively clear fluid above — the fluid above the boundary looks noticeably less cloudy than the original lysate did before spinning.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Centrifuging a cell lysate applies centrifugal force that sediments the denser cellular debris into a compact pellet at the bottom of the tube's conical tip, while the less dense, soluble components stay suspended in the clarified supernatant fluid above it; because the spin has already run to completion, this separation is already fully formed by the time the tube is removed and held upright.

subject: Biophysics
selected_point: Protein precipitation, resulting in the formation and sedimentation of visible solids from the solution.
posted_prompt: On the experimental bench, a transparent beaker containing cell-free microbial culture medium was gently stirred, and then a concentrated salt solution was added. After stopping the stirring, the beaker was left undisturbed.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Salt-induced protein precipitation in cell-free biological solution.
Minimum mechanism: Proteins must be present and soluble pre-addition; salt must be added post-stirring to ensure mixing-driven supersaturation; gravitational settling requires sufficient particle size/mass and time for Brownian motion to be overcome.
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0–2] Beaker with clear medium at rest → [Frame 3–4] Gentle stirring creates transient vortex → [Frame 5] Stir rod fully withdrawn → [Frame 6] Salt solution contacts surface → [Frame 7–8] Localized turbidity appears at interface → [Frame 9–10] Turbidity expands downward, then discrete particles descend → [Frame 11–15] Particles accumulate at base, forming sharp sediment-supernatant boundary; all phases observed from fixed frontal bench-level perspective with unobstructed view of full beaker height.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place transparent cylindrical beaker containing clear, colorless-to-pale-amber cell-free microbial culture medium on bench.
2. Gently stir medium with clean stir rod for ≤2 seconds.
3. Remove stir rod, then add concentrated salt solution dropwise to center of liquid surface.
4. Cease all motion; leave beaker undisturbed.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
White or off-white particulate solids form at liquid-salt interface, then descend continuously under gravity and accumulate as a compact, level sediment layer at the beaker bottom; supernatant above becomes fully transparent.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Protein precipitation: addition of high-concentration salt disrupts hydration shells and electrostatic repulsion, reducing protein solubility and causing aggregation into visible, sedimentable solids.

subject: Atmospheric Science
selected_point: A cooled surface plate comes into contact with warm, moist air, forming a visible fog layer.
posted_prompt: A cold, flat metal plate placed on a table is gently blown over by warm, humid air.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Surface condensation of water vapor due to thermal contact between unsaturated warm humid air and a sub-dew-point cold surface.
Minimum mechanism: Plate temperature must be below dew point of incoming air; air must contain sufficient water vapor; surface must be thermally conductive and non-porous to enable rapid heat transfer and droplet nucleation.
(ii)Storyline: [Phase 1] Static shot: cold metal plate resting undisturbed on tabletop. [Phase 2] Airflow initiation: humid air source enters frame from side and makes contact with plate upper surface. [Phase 3] Immediate response: fog layer appears uniformly across plate surface *only during* airflow. [Phase 4] Cessation: airflow ends → fog vanishes fully within same continuous shot. Experimental Procedure
1. Place a clean, flat, metallic plate on a dry tabletop.
2. Generate warm, humid air (e.g., via human exhalation or humidifier nozzle) and direct it gently across the upper surface of the plate.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
A thin, uniform, whitish, semi-transparent fog layer forms instantly on the plate surface during airflow and vanishes completely within 1 second after airflow stops.
Summary of Experimental Principles
When warm, moisture-laden air contacts a cooled surface, water vapor condenses into microscopic liquid droplets, forming visible fog—a phase change driven by temperature differential and surface nucleation.

subject: Atmospheric Science
selected_point: Cloud in a Bottle: Condensation Caused by Pressure Release
posted_prompt: A sealed, transparent plastic bottle with a small pool of water at its base and clear air inside is squeezed firmly by hand and then suddenly released.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Adiabatic cooling-driven condensation via rapid pressure release in saturated air.
Minimum mechanism: Air inside the sealed bottle must already be saturated with water vapor before squeezing; squeezing must compress and slightly warm this air without producing visible condensation; the instantaneous release must cause rapid expansion and cooling of the air, driving it past saturation (supersaturation) so that water vapor condenses onto ambient dust and aerosol particles naturally present in the air (heterogeneous nucleation), forming visible liquid droplets.
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0–2s] Bottle stationary, capped, interior air appears clear with a small pool of water visible at the base → [Frame 2–3s] Hands approach and make contact with the bottle → [Frame 3–4s] Bottle walls visibly buckle inward symmetrically → [Frame 4s] Release begins → [Frame 4–4.5s] White cloud appears centrally within the bottle volume, expanding radially → [Frame 4.5–7s] Cloud maintains defined boundaries and uniform density → [Frame 7–10s] Cloud gradually fades without splitting or streaking; bottle remains fully visible in fixed side-view throughout.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Fill a transparent plastic bottle with ~10 mL water, cap tightly.
2. Shake gently for 2 seconds to saturate air with water vapor.
3. Squeeze bottle firmly until walls visibly buckle inward.
4. Hold squeeze for <1 second, then release instantly.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
A white, translucent cloud forms inside the bottle immediately upon release and dissipates within ~5 seconds. No cloud forms during squeezing or before release.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Rapid adiabatic expansion cools the saturated air inside the bottle below its dew point. The resulting supersaturated water vapor condenses onto ambient dust and aerosol particles naturally present in the air (heterogeneous nucleation), forming the microscopic liquid droplets seen as a visible cloud.

subject: Earth Science
selected_point: Tank with an immersed vibration source generating surface ripples
posted_prompt: A clear tank with a small vibration source fixed at the central position just below the water surface; it continuously transmits vibrations into the water when activated.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Mechanical surface wave generation via immersed point source in a bounded liquid medium.
Minimum mechanism: A sustained, localized oscillation beneath the water surface must couple energy into the air-water interface, producing outward-propagating transverse disturbances that obey radial symmetry and amplitude decay—requiring immobile source, quiescent initial state, and absence of confounding forces (e.g., wind, currents, container resonance).
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0–2] Still water surface, centered submerged source visible through tank wall; [Frame 3–4] First ripple crest appears at center; [Frame 5–8] Ripples expand continuously as concentric circles at a steady outward speed, maintaining circular symmetry and a consistent spacing between adjacent rings; [Frame 9–10] Ripple propagation continues smoothly with visible amplitude decay toward edges; all phases viewed from fixed frontal/slightly elevated perspective ensuring full visibility of water surface and central source location.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Fill a clear rectangular glass tank with still water to 80% height.
2. Fix a small mechanical vibration source (e.g., miniature speaker or piezoelectric actuator) so that it sits horizontally centered in the tank and just below the water surface, without touching the tank bottom.
3. Activate the source to generate continuous vibrations.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
Concentric circular ripples emerge continuously from the center of the water surface and propagate outward symmetrically; ripples remain confined to the water-air interface with no splashing or subsurface disturbance.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Mechanical wave generation: A localized periodic disturbance in an elastic medium (water) produces transverse surface waves; wavefronts expand radially due to isotropic propagation in a homogeneous, bounded 2D surface layer.

subject: Earth Science
selected_point: The mineralization process of fossilized organisms
posted_prompt: A porous sponge sample was placed in a beaker. Calcium carbonate solution was then gradually poured in until the sponge's base was fully submerged.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Capillary-driven infiltration of aqueous mineral solution into a biogenic porous substrate as the first mechanistic step in permineralization.
Minimum mechanism: Solution must be miscible with water, low-viscosity, and chemically inert toward sponge collagen/chitin; sponge must possess open, interconnected porosity to permit bulk fluid entry; gravity and capillary pressure must jointly drive vertical wetting front progression.
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0–2] Dry sponge placed centrally in beaker → [Frame 3–4] Solution poured, contacting sponge base → [Frame 5–10] Wetting front visibly advances upward *within* pore lumens (not just surface coating), evidenced by progressive darkening confined to pore pathways; view remains fixed frontal-macro (no zoom/pan), ensuring full sponge-beaker spatial relationship is continuously visible; no time-lapse or accelerated change — only real-time infiltration dynamics observable in 10s.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place dry porous sponge sample upright in clear glass beaker.
2. Slowly pour colorless calcium carbonate solution into beaker until base of sponge is submerged.
3. Observe immediate infiltration of solution into sponge pores.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
Solution advances upward through interconnected pores, causing localized darkening and increased opacity within pore channels — no surface crystallization, no bubbling, no dissolution.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Calcium carbonate solution infiltrates porous matrix via capillary action; this simulates early-stage mineralization where dissolved ions enter void spaces of organic templates — prerequisite for later fossilization via precipitation and replacement.

pg_specification.level_1: No sponge is visible, no beaker is shown, and no liquid is poured; the scene bears no resemblance to a sponge placed in a beaker of solution.

subject: Geology & Geophysics
selected_point: Erosion simulation: Water flow over soil and gravel
posted_prompt: A small tray with a slight inclination contains soil and small pebbles. Water is continuously poured from the higher end, causing the water to flow across the tray and exit from the lower side.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Fluvial erosion driven by gravity-driven surface runoff on an inclined sediment bed.
Minimum mechanism: Water must exert shear stress sufficient to overcome sediment cohesion/friction; soil must be unconsolidated and erodible; pebbles must be small enough to be entrained by flow at observed velocity; inclination must provide unidirectional flow vector.
(ii)Storyline: [Phase 1] Dry tray with static soil+pebbles establishes baseline state. [Phase 2] Water introduced at higher end initiates wetting front propagation. [Phase 3] Wetting front reaches soil → reduced cohesion → particle detachment. [Phase 4] Flow velocity increases downslope → pebbles begin rolling/sliding. [Phase 5] Sediment transport concentrates near lower exit → visible accumulation/channel incision. Perspective: Fixed frontal/slightly elevated view showing full tray length; no occlusion; all phases visible in sequence without cuts or viewpoint shifts.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place a rectangular tray on a stable surface with slight, fixed inclination (higher end raised).
2. Spread a layer of dry soil evenly across tray bottom, then scatter small, rounded pebbles over soil.
3. Pour water continuously from a fixed point at the higher end, allowing it to flow down the tray and exit solely at the lower end.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
- Water advances as a coherent wetting front from higher to lower end.
- Soil particles detach and move downstream with flow.
- Pebbles roll or slide in direction of flow, not against it.
- Erosion intensifies near lower end; sediment accumulates or channels form there.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Water flow over inclined soil and gravel demonstrates fluvial erosion: gravitational potential energy drives flow, shear stress mobilizes sediment, and transport capacity depends on flow velocity and particle size.

subject: Geology & Geophysics
selected_point: Mineral fluorescence under ultraviolet light (calcite or fluorite luminescence)
posted_prompt: In a dark room, place a calcite or fluorite mineral on the table and repeatedly expose it to a handheld ultraviolet lamp by turning it on and off.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Instantaneous, reversible, UV-triggered visible luminescence from mineral activators.
Minimum mechanism: UV photons are absorbed by activator ions within the crystal lattice (e.g., Mn²⁺ or rare-earth ions substituted into the calcite or fluorite structure) → electrons in these activator ions are excited to higher energy states → rapid radiative relaxation back to the ground state → visible photons emitted; zero delay or persistence beyond the moment of UV exposure; emission spectrum determined solely by activator identity and host lattice.
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0–t1] Dark room, static table, inert mineral visible in ambient blackness. → [t1] Hand enters frame holding UV lamp, positions it near mineral (no contact). → [t2] Lamp switches ON → immediate onset of colored surface glow *only on mineral*. → [t3] Lamp switches OFF → glow vanishes within one frame. → [t4] Lamp switches ON again → identical glow reappears. → [t5] Lamp switches OFF again → glow vanishes identically. Throughout: fixed viewpoint, no camera motion, no ambient light intrusion, no object displacement, no emission outside mineral boundary.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place a calcite or fluorite mineral specimen on a table in a completely dark room.
2. Hold a handheld longwave ultraviolet (365 nm) lamp near the mineral.
3. Turn the lamp on → observe fluorescence → turn lamp off → observe fluorescence ceasing.
4. Repeat the on/off cycle at least twice.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
When UV lamp is ON: mineral emits visible colored light (e.g., red/orange for calcite; blue/violet for fluorite) — self-luminous, surface-localized, no persistence.
When UV lamp is OFF: emitted light disappears immediately; mineral returns to inert, non-glowing state; no afterglow or residual color.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Fluorescence is photon absorption at UV wavelength followed by near-instantaneous re-emission at longer visible wavelengths. Calcite and fluorite contain activator impurities (e.g., Mn²⁺, rare earths) that enable this process. Emission ceases within nanoseconds of UV removal — no phosphorescence.

subject: Marine Science
selected_point: Oil spreads on the water surface and covers a feather.
posted_prompt: In a shallow seawater tray, dark crude oil was poured onto the water surface, with a clean bird feather floating nearby. The water surface was gently disturbed by slow hand movements.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Interfacial fluid displacement driven by surface-wave momentum transfer causes a floating oil film to advance across a water surface until it engulfs a floating object in its path, illustrating how surface oil contamination reaches and coats objects such as seabirds' feathers.
Minimum mechanism: Oil must remain a contiguous, non-wetting surface film; water must sustain propagating waves generated by the hand motion rather than by direct hand contact with the oil or feather; the feather must act as a passive, buoyant marker until the oil reaches it; wave-driven advance of the oil film must eventually bring its leading edge into contact with the feather and visibly coat its surface.
(ii) Storyline: [Frame 0–2] Oil poured → forms a static circular patch; feather placed nearby, stationary and clean. [Frame 3–4] Hand enters frame, begins a slow horizontal sweep → ripples initiate at the water surface near the hand. [Frame 5–7] Ripples propagate outward → the oil film deforms and spreads concentrically toward the feather while staying cohesive. [Frame 8–10] The oil film's leading edge reaches the feather, and the feather's surface becomes visibly darkened and coated where the oil touches it; ripples dampen gradually; all other spatial relationships within the tray stay unchanged. Perspective: Fixed overhead or 30° oblique view, level with the water surface; full tray visible; no occlusion; lighting reveals oil iridescence and the contrast between the feather's clean and oil-coated regions.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Fill a shallow transparent tray with clear seawater to about 2 cm depth.
2. Gently pour dark crude oil onto the center of the water surface.
3. Place a clean white bird feather a few centimeters from the oil patch, floating freely.
4. With a hand held just above the water surface, make slow, horizontal sweeping motions to generate gentle ripples.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
- The dark oil forms a cohesive, iridescent film that spreads radially across the water surface.
- The feather stays clean and afloat while the ripples reach it, but once the advancing oil film's edge reaches the feather, the feather's surface becomes visibly coated and darkened by the oil.
- Ripples propagate outward from the hand's motion and visibly push the oil film ahead of them until it reaches and engulfs the feather.
Summary of Experimental Principles
- Oil is hydrophobic and less dense than seawater, so it forms a film on the surface rather than mixing in.
- Surface tension and viscosity govern how fast and how continuously the oil spreads.
- Mechanical disturbance from the hand transfers momentum to the water and then to the oil film, driving its lateral displacement until it reaches and coats objects such as the feather — the same mechanism by which oil spills contaminate wildlife at sea.

subject: Archaeology
selected_point: Pore-Related Water Absorption of Pottery Shards with Visible Bubbles
posted_prompt: Immerse a dry, unglazed ceramic shard in a glass container filled with clear, still water and allow it to stand for several minutes.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Capillary-driven water absorption into interconnected micropores of low-fired unglazed ceramic, with trapped pore air visibly escaping as bubbles during uptake.
Minimum mechanism: Ceramic must be porous and hydrophilic; water must be pure and still; surface tension and pore radius must permit spontaneous imbibition; air previously trapped inside the pores is displaced as water enters, which can appear as small bubbles released from the shard's surface; no surface sealant or glaze blocking pore access.
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0] Dry shard positioned adjacent to full glass container with still water surface → [Contact onset] Shard touches water surface, initiating meniscus rise → [Absorption onset] Localized darkening begins at the water-contact zone, often accompanied by small air bubbles escaping from the shard's surface as displaced pore air rises → [Propagation phase] Darkening spreads continuously across immersed surface without reversal or patchiness, with bubble release tapering off as saturation progresses → [Stabilization] Surface fully darkened, bubbling has ceased, water undisturbed, shard motionless, all under fixed viewpoint with no extraneous interference.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place dry, unglazed ceramic shard beside a transparent glass container filled with clear, still water.
2. Gently lower shard vertically into water until fully submerged.
3. Hold still for observation (no motion for remainder of clip).
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
Shard surface visibly darkens progressively after water contact, beginning at the immersion point and spreading across the immersed area; small air bubbles are released from the shard's pores as water displaces trapped air, most noticeable in the first seconds of contact and tapering off as saturation proceeds; water remains otherwise clear and undisturbed.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Pore-related water absorption in pottery shards: unglazed ceramic contains interconnected micropores; capillary action draws water into these pores, displacing air that was trapped inside (visible as bubbles escaping from the surface) while increasing light absorption and causing surface darkening — both are diagnostic indicators of porosity and firing conditions in archaeological ceramic analysis.

subject: Geography
selected_point: Chemical Weathering: Karst Dissolution in Guilin (Limestone Peak Forest, Conical) vs. Karst Dissolution in Croatia (Limestone Pillar Forest, Columnar)
posted_prompt: The video first presents the karst dissolution landscape in Guilin, followed by the karst dissolution landscape in Croatia. The focus is on the differences in morphology between these two limestone landscapes.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Visual differentiation of two end-member karst morphologies formed by dissolutional weathering of limestone under contrasting environmental controls.
Minimum mechanism: Limestone must be visibly bare or sparsely vegetated; morphology must arise from solutional shaping (not collapse, tectonics, or erosion), requiring smooth, rounded, or vertically grooved surfaces without mechanical breakage signatures.
(ii)Storyline: Frame 1–5: Stable wide shot of Guilin landscape: conical peaks dominate, evenly spaced, soft contours, flat base plane visible. Frame 6–7: Seamless transition (cut/fade/pan) preserving horizon and scale. Frame 8–10: Stable wide shot of Croatian landscape: slender pillars stand in isolation, tall and straight, with deep shadowed corridors between them; ground plane remains level and exposed. Perspective must be consistent (oblique aerial, ~30° angle), no close-ups or rotating views; visibility requires full silhouette definition against sky/ground: no fog, haze, or occlusion.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Show aerial or oblique view of Guilin karst: clustered, isolated, conical limestone peaks rising from flat alluvial plain.
2. Transition to aerial or oblique view of Croatian karst: scattered, isolated, slender, columnar limestone pillars rising from karstified plateau.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
- Guilin: conical, rounded, symmetrical peaks with gentle lower slopes and clustered distribution.
- Croatia: tall, narrow, vertically oriented pillars with high height-to-width ratio and wide inter-pillar spacing.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Chemical weathering (carbonic acid dissolution) is the primary shaper of both landscapes, though the resulting morphology differs with climate, lithology, and structural control. Guilin's thick, pure, flat-lying limestone in a humid subtropical climate dissolves broadly across bedding surfaces, rounding isolated blocks into a widespread field of clustered conical peaks rising from a flat alluvial plain. In Croatia's Dinaric karst, dissolution instead concentrates along closely spaced, near-vertical joint sets within thick limestone, producing isolated, slender limestone pillars with a high height-to-width ratio; this fully columnar relief is more localized to specific structurally-controlled sectors of the plateau, rather than characterizing the entire karst region the way conical peak forests dominate the Guilin landscape.
